def.en: Digital transformation requires changed mindsets and adapted work processes throughout the organisation.

short.en: working with the help of digital devices, tools and platforms

def.en: Digital working makes it easier to access stored documents from anywhere and edit shared files in real time.

short.en: the ability of computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, e.g. learning, drawing conclusions or understanding language

def.en: Artificial intelligence is based on trained models that can identify patterns from processed data.

short.en: a precisely defined sequence of steps or rules by which a computer or AI solves a problem

def.en: A developed algorithm can generate personalised recommendations from collected user data.

short.en: the use of technology to complete tasks without human intervention

def.en: Automation makes it possible to complete recurring tasks more efficiently using programmed machines.

short.en: a branch of AI in which computers learn from data and improve themselves

def.en: In machine learning, collected data is used to develop improved predictive models.

short.en: the systematic examination of data to find patterns or insights

def.en: Through data analysis, collected information can be converted into usable insights for strategic decisions.

short.en: all measures that ensure personal data is handled securely and confidentially

def.en: Data protection means that stored user data may only be used for permitted purposes.

short.en: european law on the protection of personal data

def.en: The GDPR prescribes how collected personal data must be secured and processed.

short.en: an internet-based storage that can be accessed from anywhere

def.en: In the cloud, shared documents and secured backups can be stored safely.

short.en: all measures to protect digital systems, networks and data from attacks

def.en: Cybersecurity includes the protection of networked systems against unauthorised access and data misuse.

short.en: a targeted attack on digital systems, networks or data by hackers

def.en: A cyberattack on networked corporate servers can cause significant damage to stored data.

short.en: a secret sequence of characters that protects access to a system or account

def.en: A securely chosen password should consist of randomly combined characters and be changed regularly.

short.en: a security procedure in which one must identify oneself using two different methods

def.en: Two-factor authentication offers increased protection against stolen passwords.

short.en: a process that converts data into an unreadable code that can only be decrypted with the correct key

def.en: <g>Encrypted</g> messages can only be read by <g>authorised</g> recipients with the matching key.

short.en: a security copy of data that can be restored in the event of a loss

def.en: A secured backup of all stored files protects the company from data loss due to technical failures.

short.en: a powerful computer that stores data and makes it available to other computers in the network

def.en: On the server, all stored company data is managed centrally in a secured environment.

short.en: the connection point between two systems, programmes or a programme and the user

def.en: A user-friendly designed interface makes it easier to operate even newly installed applications.

short.en: all programmes and applications running on a computer or device

def.en: Regularly updated software protects against known security vulnerabilities and improves system performance.

short.en: the physical components of a computer or device, e.g. screen, keyboard or processor

def.en: The outdated hardware must be replaced with more powerful devices so that the system runs smoothly.

short.en: a new, improved version of a programme or operating system

def.en: A regularly installed update fixes known errors and adds improved functions.

short.en: software or an app that helps with work, e.g. for communication, project planning or data management

def.en: A well-chosen digital tool can significantly simplify time-consuming tasks.

short.en: a digital environment in which users can create, share or communicate content

def.en: A widely used platform offers networked teams the possibility of collaborating in real time.

short.en: the connection of devices, systems or people via a network

def.en: Thanks to networking, globally distributed teams can access shared resources.

short.en: the structured sequence of tasks and steps in a work process

def.en: A clearly defined workflow reduces unnecessarily occurring waiting times and improves team efficiency.

short.en: software that supports teams in planning, tracking and coordinating projects

def.en: A cloud-based project management tool makes it possible to assign tasks to distributed teams in real time.

short.en: to work from a location other than the office, often from home

def.en: Working remotely requires stable internet connections and well-equipped home workspaces.

short.en: a data analysis in which artificial intelligence is used to gain insights faster and more precisely

def.en: AI-supported analysis provides precise recommendations for action on the basis of processed data.

short.en: the worldwide process of economic, political and cultural interconnection

def.en: Globalisation has created globally networked markets and produced internationally active companies.

short.en: something that concerns or crosses several countries

def.en: An <g>internationally positioned</g> company must address <g>different</g> regulations and cultures.

short.en: the official language used in a company for internal and external communication

def.en: In internationally active companies, English is often the uniformly used corporate language.

short.en: a language that is not a person's mother tongue

def.en: Well-trained specialists master at least one foreign language and can communicate in international teams.

short.en: a person for whom a particular language is their mother tongue

def.en: A natively shaped native speaker uses linguistic nuances that often remain hidden from learned speakers.

short.en: difficulties in communication due to different languages or language skills

def.en: An existing language barrier can lead to misunderstandings in multinationally staffed teams.

short.en: a misunderstanding arising from different cultural expectations or communication styles

def.en: A culturally caused intercultural misunderstanding can lead to conflicts in internationally composed teams.

short.en: a journey undertaken for professional reasons

def.en: On a business trip to a rapidly growing country, one should inform oneself about locally applicable business practices.

short.en: an internship completed in another country to gain international experience

def.en: An internship abroad in an internationally renowned company is an enriching experience.

short.en: the collaboration of people or organisations from different countries

def.en: Successfully conducted international cooperation requires clearly defined communication channels.

short.en: the central office or main administration of a company

def.en: At the headquarters in Frankfurt, all globally made decisions are coordinated and centrally managed.

short.en: a company that is legally independent but controlled by a parent company

def.en: The subsidiary founded abroad allows the corporation to open up new markets without relocating the entire operation overseas.

short.en: an organisation that represents the interests of businesses in a region and advises companies

def.en: The regionally active chamber of commerce offers companies advice on funding programmes, foreign trade and start-up questions.

short.en: to sell and deliver goods or services to foreign countries

def.en: The company specialised in renewable energies exports its technologies to over 40 countries and is considered leading internationally.

short.en: to buy goods or services from abroad and bring them into one's own country

def.en: The manufacturing industry imports numerous required raw materials from countries where they are more cost-effectively extracted.

short.en: a country or company with which goods or services are regularly exchanged

def.en: China is one of Germany's most significant trading partners in the fields of mechanical engineering and electronics.

short.en: a government tax on imported or exported goods; also the authority that controls this

def.en: The customs duties arising at the border crossing can significantly increase import costs and must be taken into account when calculating the selling price.

short.en: all the steps and actors involved in the production and delivery of a product from raw material to end customer

def.en: A disrupted supply chain can result in required components not arriving on time and production coming to a standstill.

short.en: the planning, control and monitoring of all processes along the supply chain to ensure efficiency and quality

def.en: A digitalised supply chain management enables companies to identify emerging bottlenecks at an early stage and take countermeasures.

short.en: the price at which one currency can be exchanged for another

def.en: A fluctuating exchange rate represents an increased financial risk for exporting companies, which can be minimised through appropriate hedging strategies.

short.en: the risk of financial losses due to unexpected fluctuations in the exchange rate

def.en: The underestimated currency risk can considerably affect international business if the agreed currency depreciates sharply against the home currency.

short.en: a place or system where supply and demand meet and prices are formed

def.en: The saturated European market forces many companies to open up new sales regions and adapt their products to changed customer needs.

short.en: the specific market or customer group that a company targets with its products or services

def.en: Before entering the market, the company must thoroughly analyse the targeted target market in order to realistically assess existing risks and opportunities.

short.en: the growth of a company through entry into new markets, locations or business areas

def.en: The planned international expansion requires well-trained managers who are familiar with the specific requirements of the target markets.

short.en: the relationship of rivalry between companies offering similar products or services on the same market

def.en: The intensified international competition forces companies to continuously develop their offered products and reduce costs.

short.en: a company or person offering similar products or services on the same market

def.en: The newly founded competitor relies on automated processes and can therefore offer lower prices than the established providers.

short.en: the ability of a company or country to compete successfully against others on the market

def.en: The increased competitiveness of the company is the result of purposefully deployed innovations and a modernised production infrastructure.

short.en: an economic area in which goods, services, capital and people can move freely, e.g. the EU single market

def.en: The unified European single market creates simplified conditions for companies, as uniform rules apply to all member states.

short.en: an official organisation that advises and supports german companies entering foreign markets

def.en: The chamber of foreign trade based abroad connects interested companies with local partners and helps to overcome bureaucratic hurdles when entering the market.

short.en: a principle by which today's needs are met in a way that gives future generations the same opportunities

def.en: While many companies regard sustainability as a cost factor, forward-looking managers see it as a long-term investment in competitiveness.

short.en: the obligation of companies or individuals to minimise the environmental impact of their actions

def.en: While environmental responsibility was often voluntary in the past, it is increasingly becoming an obligation for all companies due to tightened legal regulations.

short.en: the total amount of greenhouse gases caused by an activity, product or organisation

def.en: While large industrial companies leave a particularly high carbon footprint as a result of decades-long production, many strive for ambitious climate protection targets.

short.en: to reduce the output of pollutants or greenhouse gases through technical or organisational measures

def.en: While some countries prefer voluntary measures, the EU legally obliges companies to reduce emissions considerably by 2030.

short.en: energy sources that renew naturally and are not depleted, e.g. sun, wind and water

def.en: While the expansion of renewable energies is progressing rapidly in northern Europe, other regions are still struggling with outdated infrastructure and missing investment.

short.en: the ratio between the benefit of an activity and the energy consumed for it — the less energy for the same result, the better

def.en: Due to rising energy costs, more and more companies are investing in improving their energy efficiency in order to save costs in the long term.

short.en: designed or carried out in a way that uses as few natural resources such as water, energy or raw materials as possible

def.en: While resource-efficient production processes initially require higher investment, they pay off in the long term as a result of reduced operating costs.

short.en: the processing of waste materials in order to reuse them as new raw materials or products

def.en: While recycling is still voluntary in many countries, the EU prescribes increasingly higher quotas for certain materials according to stricter legislation.

short.en: an economic model in which products and materials are used, repaired and recycled for as long as possible to minimise waste

def.en: The circular economy is gaining importance due to increasing resource scarcity, while the conventional linear model of produce–use–discard is reaching its limits.

short.en: the obligation of companies or individuals to contribute to the welfare of society beyond their own profit

def.en: Social responsibility, according to growing expectations, goes beyond mere donations and encompasses fair working conditions throughout the entire business operation.

short.en: the voluntary commitment of companies to social, environmental and ethical goals that goes beyond legal minimum requirements

def.en: While CSR was often considered a voluntary extra in the past, it is becoming a strategic factor due to changed consumer expectations and tightened regulations.

short.en: a law that obliges companies to comply with and monitor human rights and environmental standards throughout their entire supply chain

def.en: Due to the supply chain due diligence act, affected companies must carefully vet their used suppliers, while significant fines threaten in the event of violations.

short.en: a trading system that guarantees fair prices and better working conditions for producers in developing countries

def.en: While conventional trade structures often come at the expense of disadvantaged producers, fair trade creates fairer conditions in favour of local communities.

short.en: a written set of rules that specifies how employees or companies should behave in certain situations

def.en: Due to increased compliance requirements, the company has introduced a code of conduct, while violations of it entail disciplinary consequences.

short.en: the principles and values according to which a company acts and makes decisions in order to act in a morally responsible way

def.en: Business ethics is gaining importance due to growing societal expectations, while companies without clearly defined values are increasingly coming under public pressure.

short.en: adherence by a company to all legal regulations, internal guidelines and ethical standards

def.en: To avoid penalties, the Compliance department strictly monitors adherence to all new guidelines.

short.en: the abuse of a position of power for personal gain, e.g. through bribery or fraud

def.en: Corruption damages the economy in the long term, as fair competitive conditions are undermined due to lack of transparency, while honest companies are disadvantaged.

short.en: the offering or accepting of money or benefits to induce someone to perform a specific, often illegal action

def.en: Bribery is a criminal offence in Germany, and due to tightened anti-corruption laws, substantial penalties threaten companies and individuals.

short.en: the reporting of misconduct, legal violations or unethical behaviour within an organisation by an insider

def.en: While whistleblowing often entailed professional disadvantages in the past, the EU now offers affected persons better legal protection due to new directives.

short.en: a person who draws attention internally or publicly to misconduct, fraud or legal violations in an organisation

def.en: The whistleblower reported the uncovered misconduct anonymously, while the company had to be contacted externally due to a lack of internal reporting channels.

short.en: the principle that all people should have equal rights and opportunities regardless of gender, origin or other characteristics

def.en: While equal treatment of women and men is a stated goal in many companies, practice often shows considerable gaps due to structural barriers.

short.en: the variety of people in an organisation in terms of gender, origin, age, abilities or other characteristics

def.en: Due to proven advantages, many companies invest in diversity, while homogeneously composed teams often develop fewer creative solutions.

short.en: the principle that all people — regardless of their abilities or differences — participate equally in social and professional life

def.en: While integration means adapting people, inclusion demands that structures are designed from the outset so that everyone can participate.

short.en: the design of environments, products and services so that they can be used by all people — regardless of physical or other limitations

def.en: Due to new EU directives, digital products and public buildings must in future meet stricter requirements for accessibility.

short.en: the principle that all people have the same access to education, careers and social participation regardless of origin, gender or social status

def.en: Equal opportunities have not yet been fully achieved despite existing laws, while structural disadvantages in education and employment continue to exist.

short.en: measures and laws intended to prevent people from being disadvantaged on the basis of characteristics such as origin, gender or religion

def.en: Anti-discrimination is more important than ever due to increasing social diversity, while companies are obliged to actively implement corresponding measures.

short.en: a german law that prohibits discrimination on the grounds of race, gender, religion, disability, age or sexual orientation

def.en: Due to the General Equal Treatment Act, employers must avoid discriminatory job advertisements, while those affected have the right to claim damages.

short.en: the obligation of a company not only to pursue economic goals but also to assume social, environmental and ethical responsibility

def.en: Corporate responsibility today encompasses far more than profit maximisation: due to growing demands, companies must also act socially and ecologically.

short.en: a gas in the atmosphere that retains heat and thus contributes to the greenhouse effect and global warming, e.g. CO2 or methane

def.en: While CO2 is the best-known greenhouse gas, methane and nitrous oxide also contribute considerably to global warming due to their higher warming effect.

short.en: the legal obligation of companies to report regularly on their economic, social or ecological activities

def.en: Due to expanded EU transparency rules, the reporting obligation for sustainability will in future also apply to medium-sized companies, while previously only corporations were affected.

short.en: a collective term for changes in the world of work driven by digitalisation, automation and new work models

def.en: The future of work is shaped by growing automation, while due to demographic change a shortage of skilled workers is simultaneously emerging.

short.en: a concept for a changed world of work that prioritises self-determination, flexibility and meaningful activity

def.en: New Work is gaining importance due to growing demands for self-determination and work-life balance, while rigid hierarchies and fixed working hours are increasingly being questioned.

short.en: a flexible, iterative way of working in which teams work in short cycles, respond quickly to changes and continuously improve

def.en: Agile working enables teams to flexibly change course during ongoing projects and to learn quickly and improve results due to regular feedback loops.

short.en: a project management approach that relies on flexibility, collaboration and incremental improvement rather than rigid plans

def.en: Agile methods rely on regular consultation with the customer during the project, due to which adjustments can be made at an early stage.

short.en: an agile framework in which teams work in short cycles (sprints), hold daily brief meetings and manage tasks in a backlog

def.en: Scrum is a widely used agile framework; during the sprint, clearly defined tasks are completed and due to the regular reviews, they are continuously improved.

short.en: an agile method for visualising workflows on a board with columns such as „to do“, „in progress“ and „done“

def.en: Kanban makes ongoing tasks visible to the whole team, while the limited number of simultaneous tasks prevents bottlenecks due to the WIP limit.

short.en: a short, time-limited work cycle in agile methods (usually 1–4 weeks) in which the team achieves a <g>defined</g> goal

def.en: During a sprint, the team concentrates on clearly defined tasks, due to which a deliverable result stands at the end.

short.en: able to plan, prioritise and carry out one’s own work independently without constant external instruction

def.en: Self-organised teams work independently during the sprint and often achieve better results due to their high degree of autonomy than strictly managed groups.

short.en: the ability of an organisation to react quickly and flexibly to changes and to adapt

def.en: Agility is today one of the most sought-after core competencies, while companies must respond more flexibly than ever due to rapidly changed market conditions.

short.en: an organisational structure with few management levels, in which decisions are made decentrally and closer to employees

def.en: Flat hierarchies foster innovation, while decisions can be made faster due to shorter communication channels than in strictly hierarchically structured organisations.

short.en: an ordered ranking of people or levels in an organisation, in which higher levels have decision-making authority over lower ones

def.en: While steep hierarchies create clear responsibilities, they slow down the organisation’s responsiveness due to long decision-making paths.

short.en: the way in which managers interact with employees, communicate and make decisions — shaped by the values and self-image of the organisation

def.en: Leadership culture is changing considerably during the digital transformation: due to growing complexity, managers are required to act more as coaches than as controllers.

short.en: a transition to new values, behaviours or ways of working in an organisation or society

def.en: Cultural change is inevitable during digitalisation, while companies must fundamentally realign their values and structures due to changed market conditions.

short.en: a new idea, method or technology that significantly improves or changes an existing process, product or industry

def.en: Innovation emerges during the interplay of creativity and willingness to take risks, while companies without continuous renewal quickly lose competitiveness due to changed market requirements.

short.en: the ability to develop original ideas and find unusual solutions to problems

def.en: Creativity is a key competency of the future, while routine tasks are increasingly being taken over by machines due to advancing automation.

short.en: a creative method for solving complex problems, in which the needs of users are at the centre

def.en: Design Thinking relies on interdisciplinary teams, while conventional problem-solving often lacks a user-centred approach due to rigid departmental boundaries.

short.en: a radical change that fundamentally replaces or supersedes existing market structures, business models or technologies

def.en: Disruption fundamentally changes entire industries during a short period of time, while established companies often react too late due to sluggish structures.

term.en: willingness to change, openness to change

short.en: the readiness to accept new things, leave familiar paths and flexibly adapt to changed conditions

def.en: Willingness to change is a key competency due to accelerated technological change, while employees without this ability are increasingly difficult to place.

short.en: a skill that is particularly in demand in the digital age, e.g. critical thinking, digital literacy or intercultural communication

def.en: Future skills are becoming increasingly important due to rapidly growing complexity in the working world, while purely technical knowledge alone is no longer sufficient.

short.en: the ability to understand and share the feelings and perspectives of other people

def.en: While machines can process data quickly, empathy is a genuinely human ability that remains irreplaceable in dealing with customers and colleagues.

short.en: acting independently and without constant external control or instruction

def.en: While in the past every decision came from a superior, autonomous working is today becoming the norm due to flat hierarchies and agile structures.

short.en: the ability to argue convincingly in negotiations, find compromises and achieve good results

def.en: While technical knowledge can be learned, negotiating skill remains an ability that only truly matures through experience due to its human complexity.

short.en: a prediction about future developments based on data or experience

def.en: While no one knows the exact future, data-based forecasts provide a sound decision-making basis due to extensive analyses.

short.en: to make contact and communicate with each other, often between humans and machines or between users and systems

def.en: While people used to communicate mainly in person, they now interact in entirely new forms due to digital platforms and AI systems.

short.en: to try something out in practice and test its suitability before deploying it widely

def.en: While the theory sounds convincing, every new concept must be tested in practice before proceeding to broad deployment due to positive results.

term.en: to relieve, to take the load off

short.en: to take work away from someone or a system and thereby reduce the load

def.en: While manual labour used to dominate everyday working life, automated systems can relieve employees today and increase productivity due to optimised processes.

term.en: to control, to manage, to steer

short.en: to direct, control or regulate something, e.g. processes, machines or information flow

def.en: While a person can control machines remotely, networked systems enable an entirely new dimension of flexibility in production due to this capability.

short.en: so clear and logical that one immediately understands and can follow the reasoning

def.en: While the statistics look complicated, the final result is clear: due to consistent digitalisation, the company was able to double its turnover.

short.en: the possibility of working from home instead of commuting to the office every day

def.en: Home office has grown considerably due to improved communication technologies, while employers and employees develop hybrid models as a proven compromise.

short.en: a work model that flexibly combines office work and working from home

def.en: Hybrid working enables greater flexibility, while companies must develop individual solutions due to varying employee needs.

short.en: a work model in which people from different companies or professions work together in a shared office or space

def.en: Coworking fosters exchange between creative professionals, while providing a cost-effective alternative to one's own office due to the shared infrastructure.

short.en: the ability to plan and organise one's own working time so that tasks are completed efficiently and on time

def.en: While distractions in the home office increase, good time management becomes more important than ever due to the lack of external structure.

short.en: the balance between professional demands and personal life that ensures long-term health and performance

def.en: Work-life balance is becoming increasingly difficult to achieve due to boundaryless work, while companies actively counter this with flexible models.

short.en: the conscious separation of work and private life in order to protect one’s own health and performance in the long term

def.en: Setting limits is difficult for many home office workers, while the lack of physical separation due to constant availability leads to a blurred transition.

short.en: the process by which new employees are introduced, integrated and prepared for their tasks in a company

def.en: While traditional onboarding took place on-site, digital onboarding requires new formats and tools due to distributed teams.

short.en: the strategy of companies to retain qualified employees in the long term, e.g. through attractive salaries, development opportunities or flexible working hours

def.en: Employee retention has become a strategic goal due to the growing shortage of skilled workers, while companies without targeted retention measures lose valuable talent.

short.en: the responsibility and effort to actively promote the well-being of people in an organisation or community

def.en: While care was previously mainly associated with the social sphere, it now encompasses occupational health programmes as well due to growing psychological burdens.

short.en: connecting various specialist fields or areas of knowledge in order to solve complex problems from multiple perspectives

def.en: Interdisciplinary collaboration often produces more innovative solutions due to different perspectives, while purely specialist teams risk thinking in their own silo.

short.en: the ability to mediate and coordinate between different specialist areas, departments or systems

def.en: Interface competency is particularly in demand due to growing complexity in networked organisations, while specialists with narrow boundaries often cannot help alone.

short.en: the ability to actively build, maintain and use professional contacts for mutual benefit

def.en: Networking competency has become a core competency during digitalisation, due to which well-connected professionals have a clear advantage on the labour market.

short.en: able to use media and digital tools critically and competently and to evaluate their content

def.en: Media-literate employees can purposefully filter relevant sources during work, due to which they make well-founded decisions.

short.en: the scientific and technical field concerned with the development, construction and deployment of robots

def.en: While robotics was previously limited to factories, autonomously working robots are now advancing into many areas of life due to falling costs and growing capabilities.

short.en: the networking of everyday objects and machines with the internet to exchange data and automate processes

def.en: The Internet of Things connects billions of connected devices, while both opportunities and security risks emerge due to the enormous volumes of data.

short.en: extremely large and complex volumes of data that can no longer be processed with conventional methods and require specialised analysis technologies

def.en: Big Data enables precise predictions and decisions due to sophisticated analysis tools, while the protection of personal data remains a central societal challenge.

short.en: a business model in which digital platforms bring together providers and users and act as intermediaries, e.g. amazon or airbnb

def.en: Platform economy is fundamentally changing established business models, while a few dominant platforms control entire markets due to digital network effects.

short.en: the concept of how a company creates, delivers and economically benefits from value

def.en: While classic business models relied on product sales, digital models are often based on data and subscriptions due to networked platforms.

short.en: designed so that it can be expanded with increasing demand or scope without fundamental changes

def.en: Scalable business models can reduce the cost per unit during growth, due to which digital companies become profitable more quickly than traditional ones.

short.en: a specific area or division in which a company is active and offers products or services

def.en: While corporations are active in many business areas simultaneously, many startups focus on one clearly defined area due to limited resources.

short.en: the totality of all impressions a person experiences when using a product or service, particularly usability and satisfaction

def.en: User experience has become the decisive differentiating feature due to growing digital competition, while poorly designed products are quickly rejected.

term.en: to operate sustainably, sustainable business practices

short.en: to run a business in a way that combines economic success with ecological responsibility and social commitment

def.en: While profit was once the only goal, sustainable business practices today form part of the standard due to changed stakeholder expectations and tightened regulation.

short.en: an announcement made over loudspeakers in a public place

def.en: Nobody in the terminal should miss an important announcement, as it concerns all passengers.

short.en: a building from which trains depart and arrive

def.en: At the train station, everyone knows that one should listen carefully to the announcements so that nobody misses the train.

short.en: a site with terminals and runways from which aircraft take off and land

def.en: At the airport, everyone should have their boarding pass ready so that nobody is held up at the gate.

short.en: when a train, flight or bus departs or arrives later than planned

def.en: In the case of a delay of more than one hour, every passenger has the right to contact someone from customer service.

short.en: another means of transport one must take after a journey to reach the destination

def.en: In the event of delays, someone from the service team is responsible for ensuring that all passengers still make their connection.

short.en: the area at the station where the train stops and passengers board and alight

def.en: At platform 7, every passenger waits patiently so that nobody is injured in the crush when boarding.

short.en: the departure of an aircraft from the airport

def.en: For departure, every passenger must be there at least two hours in advance so that nobody is left behind in the rush.

short.en: the arrival of an aircraft, train or bus at the destination

def.en: After arrival, every traveller should collect their luggage from the belt so that nothing gets lost.

short.en: the entrance at the airport through which one boards the aircraft

def.en: At gate C14, every passenger must show their boarding pass so that nobody boards the aircraft without authorisation.

short.en: suitcases, bags and other items taken on a journey

def.en: For luggage over ten kilograms, someone must check in at the counter, as one cannot stow it in the cabin baggage.

short.en: to officially register at the airport or hotel

def.en: Before anyone passes through security, one must check in online or at the counter.

short.en: to officially leave the hotel and return the key

def.en: When checking out, every guest must hand in their room key so that nobody forgets to return it.

short.en: an advance booking for a room, table or ticket

def.en: Without a confirmed reservation, nobody can be sure of getting a room if someone arrives at short notice.

short.en: to reserve a seat, room or ticket in advance

def.en: Everyone should book flights and hotels in good time so that nobody pays significantly more when searching at short notice.

short.en: a car with a driver that can be hired for journeys in exchange for payment

def.en: At the airport, everyone can find a taxi, but one should clarify the price beforehand so that nothing remains unclear.

short.en: a car hired for a certain period in exchange for a fee

def.en: With a hire car, everyone can travel flexibly without depending on someone with a fixed timetable.

short.en: an explanation of how to get from one place to another

def.en: When someone needs directions, one should explain them clearly and simply so that nobody gets lost.

short.en: no longer knowing the right way and not knowing where one is

def.en: In an unfamiliar city, one can easily get lost if nobody has a map with them.

short.en: the ability to find one's way in an unfamiliar environment

def.en: With poor orientation in an unfamiliar city, someone can ask at the hotel reception, as one always gets help there.

short.en: the time spent in a place, e.g. in a hotel or city

def.en: For a stay of more than five nights, every hotel guest receives something as a welcome gift.

short.en: a place to sleep and stay when travelling, e.g. hotel, hostel or holiday apartment

def.en: On long business trips, every employee must arrange their own accommodation unless someone from the company takes care of it.

short.en: a building with halls and rooms for conferences, meetings and events

def.en: In the conference centre, every participant finds a place as one can book the rooms in advance.

short.en: a larger, formal event at which experts or representatives of an industry come together

def.en: At the conference, every participant can get to know someone from another country.

short.en: the place where an event takes place

def.en: Every guest should be informed about the venue in advance so that nobody goes to the wrong address.

short.en: the registration desk in a hotel or at an event

def.en: At the hotel reception, every guest receives their key and can ask someone for information.

short.en: to officially register for an event or hotel

def.en: Before anyone can enter the conference, one must register at the entrance.

short.en: an organised event with a specific purpose, e.g. a congress, trade fair or company event

def.en: For the event, every participant must be registered in advance so that nobody is admitted without an invitation.

task.en:
In your company, delivery delays keep occurring because the supplier doesn't inform you reliably.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Cause: What is the main problem?
Solution: How can communication with the supplier be improved?
Timing: When should the conversation take place?
Next steps: Who takes on which task, and by when?

q.en: So, we have the challenge that delivery times keep getting delayed. I see the main problem in the fact that the supplier doesn't inform us reliably.

a.en: Did I understand you correctly: <g>it</g>'s mainly about the poor communication with the supplier?

q1.en: Exactly, that captures it well. What do you think we could do about it?

a1.en: I would suggest that we request a fixed contact person at the supplier who informs us regularly.

q2.en: That sounds sensible. Should we discuss that with the supplier this week already?

a2.en: Yes, I'll gladly arrange an appointment and send you the invitation.

q3.en: Good, then let's note down the next steps: <r>Who takes on which task? By when?</r>

a3.en: <r>The next steps are: you arrange the appointment with the supplier, I prepare the documents. Deadline: by Friday this week.</r>

task.en:
In your company, there are recurring problems with a supplier, and management needs to be informed about possible countermeasures.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would proceed in this situation.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What consequences would it have not to solve the problem?
Safeguard: How can you find a safeguard against future supply shortages?
Report: How do you prepare a report for management?
Task division: Who takes on which task, and by when?

q.en: Exactly. What consequences do you think this would have if we don't solve the problem?

a.en: What could we do in this situation? Do you have a suggestion on how we should proceed?

q1.en: I have an idea or a suggestion: we could, for example, plan a second supplier as a backup.

a1.en: <g>It</g> would make sense if we tested that in the short term. An alternative would also be to increase stock levels.

q2.en: What do you think about implementing both measures at the same time? How do you see it?

a2.en: I think that would be too much at once. From my point of view, it speaks in favor of first testing the second supplier.

q3.en: But the argument against that is that it costs us time. Would you agree to start both steps in parallel?

a3.en: That sounds convincing. I agree with that, because that way we'll find a solution faster.

q4.en: Good idea, however we should also consider that management has to agree. I see it differently: we should first prepare a short report.

a4.en: Let's note down the following points: report, cost overview and schedule. What can we agree on?

q5.en: We prioritize the report first, then the schedule. Who takes on which task? By when?

a5.en: As a compromise, we could split the tasks between the two of us. If we deliver by Friday, would that be acceptable for you?

q6.en: We could find a middle ground <g>by</g> writing the report together and creating the schedule separately.

a6.en: Let's summarize: we will write the report together. So, this is how we'll do it now: I'll take care of the schedule.

q7.en: Next steps are: finalize the report, Mr. Schmidt is responsible, deadline: Friday. What exactly do you mean by 'finalize'?

a7.en: By that I mean that all the figures <g>have been checked</g> and the document <g>has been sent</g> to management. Thank you, then we agree.

task.en:
Your company is relocating, and the new commute is much longer for many colleagues (almost 60 kilometers).

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What consequences would it have for the team if nothing is done?
Home office: Could a home office proposal help?
Flextime: Would flexible flextime be an additional solution?
Compromise: How can a compromise between office and home office be found?

q.en: We have a problem: management has decided that our location will be moved to another suburb starting next year. The distance to the new workplace is almost 60 kilometers, and many colleagues don't know now whether they should commute or relocate.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that the new location is too far away for many employees?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have for the team if we do nothing?

a1.en: <r>I think that</r> several experienced specialists would resign, because the daily commuting time would be too long for them.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> suggest to management that employees be allowed to work from home two days a week?

a2.en: That <r>certainly makes sense</r>, since then people wouldn't have to get used to a new place of residence right away. But we should first clarify whether that's even an option for all departments.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to also introduce flexible working hours with a fixed core time. <r>What do you think about that</r>?

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that not every department can work from home - accounting, for example, often needs personal contact with clients on-site.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> working alternately in the office and from home.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. I really can't imagine that management would be against it if we show that productivity doesn't decrease as a result.

q5.en: Should we also suggest making a change to the fixed-term employment contracts and converting them into permanent ones, so that the specialists feel more secure at the new location?

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>, because it builds trust. In addition, we could offer everyone who actually wants to relocate a small relocation allowance.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll prepare a short report on the home office options, and you take care of the figures for the relocation allowance. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to finish your part by Wednesday, so we still have time for corrections?

q7.en: Would it be realistic if we finish the proposal by the end of the week and present it at the meeting next Monday?

a7.en: Yes, that should be feasible if we quickly touch base again tomorrow to clarify the last details.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we're proposing flexible home office, a fair flextime arrangement, and a relocation allowance, so that nobody has to resign because of the new location.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we also meet the requirement to treat all employees fairly - our proposal will surely gain recognition from management. I'll write up the minutes and send them to you today.

task.en:
Topic: At the employment agency – „Our new colleague's social security number and work permit still haven't arrived.“

These points can help you.
Consequences: What consequences would a delay have for the team?
Interim solution: Could a temporary part-time position help?
Support: How can she be supported at the employment agency?
Task-sharing: How can accompanying her be organized within the team?

q.en: We have a problem: our new colleague, Ms. Klein, is a career changer and registered as unemployed on time, but her social security number and work permit still haven't arrived, because some documents are missing at the employment agency.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that she can't officially start with us without that number?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have for the team if she can't start on time?

a1.en: Honestly, that worries me a bit, because the project would then have to start without her and the other colleagues would have to take on extra tasks.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> make her an offer and let her work part-time at first, until all the documents are complete?

a2.en: That sounds sensible, but we should first clarify whether that's even an option without a valid work permit.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to submit a request to the employment agency about whether we can accompany her to her next appointment, so she attends it for sure and everything goes faster.

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that we'd have to free someone up during working hours for that.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> splitting the accompanying duty within the team.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. I really can't imagine that being a big problem for just one morning.

q5.en: In addition, we could reimburse her travel costs for the trips to the agency - I think she's even entitled to it, since she has to make the extra trip.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. We could also only start her probationary period from her actual start date, so she doesn't lose anything.

q6.en: Let's tackle and split up the tasks: I'll sort things out with HR, and you talk to Ms. Klein about the new schedule. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to sort that out with HR this week already?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if I get that done by Thursday and we touch base briefly again on Friday?

a7.en: That should be feasible. I'll then inform Ms. Klein about the solution on Friday afternoon.

q8.en: Let's summarize: Ms. Klein will work part-time for now, we'll accompany her to the agency, reimburse her travel costs, and postpone the start of her probationary period, so she isn't disadvantaged.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we also meet the requirement to treat new colleagues fairly - this solution will surely gain recognition from Ms. Klein. I'll summarize the key points and send them to both of you today.

task.en:
For a new client project your team needs someone with negotiation skills and experience in risk management, but right now nobody on the team has both.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What happens if the project starts without the necessary skills?
Task division: How can tasks be divided according to strengths?
Client support: Who takes over client support if tasks are reassigned?
Solution: How can the problem be solved overall?

q.en: We have a problem: for the new client project we need someone with strong negotiation skills and experience in risk management, but right now nobody on the team has both.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that internally we don't have the right combination of expertise?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if we start the project anyway without the necessary skills?

a1.en: I think that would be a bad idea, because then we wouldn't be able to react quickly enough to problems.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> split the tasks according to our strengths? You do have quite a lot of negotiation skills, don't you?

a2.en: That's true, but unfortunately I have no experience at all in risk management - it's really not my thing.

q3.en: No problem, I'm pretty strong in time management and problem solving instead - I could take that on.

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that then there'd be nobody left for customer service, since you're currently handling that too.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> having not only me, but also a colleague from the other team take over customer service.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. I don't think that would be a problem if we announce it in good time.

q5.en: In addition, we could suggest an external risk management training for you, so that next time you're not dependent on us anymore.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. By the way, I'm also not afraid of getting into a new topic.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll take care of handing over customer service, and you sign up for the risk management training. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. I don't intend to put that off - I'll sign up this week already.

q7.en: Would it be realistic if we start the project next week anyway, even if your training isn't finished yet?

a7.en: Yes, that should be no problem, as long as we don't have to make any risky decisions at the very start.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we split the tasks according to our strengths, you do the risk management training, and customer service goes not only to me, but also to a colleague from the other team.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we meet the project's requirements without either of us being overwhelmed - this solution will surely go down well with the client. I'll write up the task distribution and send it to you today. <r>Let's also get together briefly next Monday to check whether everything is going as planned.</r>

task.en:
A colleague wants to have his professional qualification, earned abroad, officially recognized, but doesn't know exactly which documents are needed for that.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you could help him.

These points can help you.
Procedure: What information is missing about the recognition procedure?
Deadlines: How can a deadline extension for missing documents help?
Funding: Which funding program could cover the costs?
Alternative: What if the qualification isn't fully recognized?

q.en: I have to quickly tell you about a colleague: Mr. Boateng <r>told me that</r> he worked as an engineer in his home country and now wants to apply for recognition of his professional qualification, but he doesn't know which documents are required for that.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that he's missing information about the procedure?

q1.en: Exactly. <r>His goal is</r> to work in his actual profession as soon as possible. What do you think, how could we help him?

a1.en: I would suggest that we contact the relevant office together and gather information for him.

q2.en: That's a good idea. By the way, he also <r>said that</r> he's still missing some documents from his home country.

a2.en: Then we should recommend that he apply for an extension of the deadline, so he can submit the missing documents calmly.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to recommend a funding programme to him - that could cover the costs of translating the documents.

a3.en: One argument in favor of that is certainly that many colleagues have already successfully made use of exactly this programme.

q4.en: True, but he also <r>mentioned that</r> he's afraid his qualification won't be fully recognized in the end.

a4.en: I understand that. But even if not everything is recognized, he could do an adaptation course <g>to</g> make up the remaining qualification.

q5.en: Good idea. I know he's very interested <g>in</g> his profession - he <r>would definitely feel like</r> doing such a course if it were necessary.

a5.en: Then we should suggest that he initiate an inquiry with the relevant office already now, even if not all the documents are complete yet.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll talk to him about his situation today, and you find out about the funding programme. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to tell him right away that we'll support him with the application?

q7.en: Yes, <r>that's exactly what I intend to do</r>. Would it be realistic if the three of us sit down the day after tomorrow to discuss everything?

a7.en: That should be feasible. I'll prepare some information about the funding programme by then.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we help Mr. Boateng with the recognition application, inform him about the funding programme and a possible adaptation course, and discuss everything together in two days.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we fulfil his wish to work in his profession again as soon as possible - that will surely help him a lot. I'll summarize the key points and send them to both of you today.

task.en:
For an open position you have already placed several job ads, but hardly any suitable applications are coming in.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you could fill the position.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What consequences would a longer vacancy have?
Headhunter: Is it worth hiring a headhunter?
Social media: What are the pros and cons of spreading it via social media?
Additional channels: Which other channels could help?

q.en: We have a problem: for the open position as a draughtsperson we've already placed three job ads on different job portals, but we've gotten <g>neither</g> enough <g>nor</g> really suitable applications.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that the classic job portals just aren't enough anymore for this position?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if we can't fill the position for even longer?

a1.en: I think that then both the colleagues on the team and our clients would suffer, because the orders would pile up.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> additionally hire a headhunter who specifically recruits suitable candidates?

a2.en: That's a good idea, but of course that costs something too - we should clarify beforehand whether it's worth it for us.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to also spread the job posting through our social network - a lot of good applications come through exactly that channel these days.

a3.en: One argument for that is certainly that it doesn't cost anything. One argument against it, though, is that we tend to reach younger target groups there who don't have a completed career path yet.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> either posting specifically in professional groups or reaching out directly to former interns.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. The more channels we use, the greater the chance of finding the right person.

q5.en: In addition, we could ask the job placement service whether they have suitable profiles.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. We should pay attention not only to technical skills, but also to the applicants' motivation.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll take care of contacting the headhunter, and you post the position on our social network. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to contact the headhunter already this week?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we already look at the first responses next week?

a7.en: A week is admittedly quite tight, but that should be feasible if both channels run at the same time.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we hire a headhunter, additionally use our social network, and ask the job placement service, so we can finally fill the position.

a8.en: Exactly. I think with this combination we have a good chance of both moving quickly and finding the right person. I'll write up the task distribution and send it to you today. <r>Let's also sit down together in two weeks to discuss the applications we've received.</r>

task.en:
A colleague's CV still needs to be revised today for an application, but the dates are inconsistent and the language skills aren't described precisely.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you could improve the CV.

These points can help you.
Impression: What impression does an inconsistent CV make?
Language levels: How can language skills be specified more precisely?
Consistent format: How can the dates be made consistent?
Implementation: How can this be done quickly and professionally?

q.en: We have a problem: we need to revise Ms. Petrenko's CV for the application today, but the dates aren't formatted consistently, and for language skills it just says 'good', without a precise level.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so it's mainly about the formatting and about giving more precise information on the language skills?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what impression does that make on a recruiter if the CV doesn't look consistent?

a1.en: I think an inconsistent tabular CV quickly looks unprofessional, even if the qualifications themselves are actually very good.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> state concrete levels for the language skills, so for example 'English: proficient to negotiation level' instead of just 'good'?

a2.en: That makes sense, but we should first ask her whether she really rates her English as negotiation-level, otherwise it looks exaggerated.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to write all the dates in the same format throughout - so either month and year everywhere, or just the year everywhere.

a3.en: One argument for that is certainly that it looks much more professional. One argument against it would be, at most, that it takes some extra time.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could solve the problem by</r> going through the template once completely and adjusting the formatting automatically.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. I can well imagine that being done in half an hour if we do it together.

q5.en: In addition, the signature under the CV is still missing - we should have her add that too.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. We could also recommend that she structure her career path a bit more clearly, with precise details on the role at each position.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll take care of the formatting and the dates, and you talk to Ms. Petrenko about the language skills and the signature. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to send her the revised version already this evening?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we're done by five p.m. so she can ask follow-up questions right away?

a7.en: That should be feasible. I'll call her right away and discuss the last details with her.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll standardize the date format, add concrete language levels and the signature, and structure the career path more clearly, so the CV looks professional.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that gives Ms. Petrenko a really professional tabular CV now - recruiters will surely respond well to that. I'll write her a quick message and send her the revised version today. <r>Let's have a quick call tomorrow morning to clarify whether she still has any questions about the application.</r>

task.en:
For two open apprenticeship places, hardly any suitable applicants have come forward so far.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you could find more trainees.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What consequences would it have not to fill the places?
Vocational school: How can contact with the vocational school help?
Pay: Should the training pay be increased?
Dual studies: Could dual studies be offered additionally?

q.en: We have a problem: we have two open apprenticeship places for the dual training as an electronics technician, but so far only two applicants have come forward, and neither of them has really shown interest in the trade.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that we can hardly find suitable apprentices for the open places?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if we can't fill the places at all this year?

a1.en: I think that then we'd be too short-staffed in the training company to handle all the tasks that come up.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> get in touch directly with the local vocational school, in order to promote our apprenticeship places there?

a2.en: That's a good idea, but we shouldn't just briefly approach the students without explaining the advantages of the dual training in detail.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to raise the trainee allowance a bit, in order to become more attractive to applicants.

a3.en: One argument for that is certainly that money matters to a lot of young people. One argument against it, though, is that we'd first have to clarify the budget for that.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps also solve the problem by</r> additionally offering a dual study programme instead of the classic apprenticeship.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. Instead of relying only on the classic apprenticeship, we should really offer both paths in parallel.

q5.en: In addition, we could look into retraining - maybe there are interested people who've already learned a different profession but want to switch.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. We should clearly communicate the goal: whoever successfully completes the dual training has good chances of being taken on permanently with us.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll take care of contacting the vocational school, and you talk to management about the trainee allowance. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to contact the vocational school already this week?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we already look at the first responses in two weeks?

a7.en: That should be feasible, as long as we start right away now, without waiting any longer.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll contact the vocational school, check on a higher trainee allowance, and additionally offer a dual study programme, in order to finally fill the open places.

a8.en: Exactly. I think with these measures we have a good chance of filling the apprenticeship places still this year. I'll write up the task distribution and send it to you today. <r>Let's also get together briefly in two weeks to discuss the first responses.</r>

task.en:
An applicant has already asked several times about the status of his unsolicited application, but you haven't reviewed his cover letter yet.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Impression: What impression does a late response leave?
Review: How can the cover letter be reviewed together quickly?
Interview: Should he be invited anyway?
Feedback: How and when should he be informed?

q.en: We have a problem: Mr. Nowak sent us an unsolicited application and has already called twice today to ask about the current status, but we haven't even properly reviewed his cover letter yet.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that we haven't been able to give him any feedback yet, even though he's already asking?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what impression does that make on him if we keep him waiting even longer?

a1.en: I think that comes across pretty badly, because a lot of applicants judge exactly that - how professional we seem as a company.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> look at his cover letter together right now and quickly decide whether it matches our job requirements profile?

a2.en: Good idea. I find his introduction strong, but his closing sentence strikes me as a bit too self-confident, almost arrogant.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to invite him to an interview anyway - in person, things like that often come across quite differently.

a3.en: One argument for that is certainly that his professional experience really fits us. One argument against it, though, is that we'd have to find a slot on short notice for that.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could solve the problem by</r> letting him know briefly today and suggesting an appointment for next week.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. Then at least he'll have a clear response and won't have to stay in the dark any longer.

q5.en: In addition, we could already mention our salary expectations for the position in the invitation, so there's clarity from the start.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. That way he can prepare better too, and tell us his own expectations in the interview.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll call him back and arrange the appointment, and you prepare the checklist for the interview. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to call him already this afternoon?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we set the appointment for Thursday already?

a7.en: That should be feasible, as long as the interview room is still free.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll call Mr. Nowak back today, invite him for an interview on Thursday, and prepare the checklist as well as our salary expectations.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we show him that we take his unsolicited application seriously - that will surely leave a good impression. I'll summarize the key points and send them to you today.

task.en: Topic: Commute – „How do you actually get to work every day?“

q.en: Tell me, how do you actually get to work every day? Do you drive or take the train?

a.en: I mostly take the train, it takes about forty minutes. Honestly, I quite like reading during that time, or I listen to a podcast. What about you, do you take the train too?

q1.en: No, I live pretty close to the office, so I mostly ride my bike when the weather cooperates. When it rains I take the bus. Doesn't <g>it</g> bother you that the ride takes so long every day?

a1.en: At first I found it pretty exhausting, but by now I've really gotten used to it. I just use the time productively. Biking sounds great too though, that must keep you fit, right?

q2.en: Yeah, totally, and it even saves me a trip to the gym. But when there's snow or ice in winter it does get a bit unpleasant sometimes.

a2.en: I can imagine. I'm glad that in winter I can just sit in the warm train and not have to worry about anything.

task.en: Topic: Weekend – „Do you already have plans for this weekend?“

q.en: Tell me, do you already have plans for this weekend?

a.en: On Saturday I'm going to the countryside with my family to visit my parents, we actually do that almost every other weekend. On Sunday though I really want to sleep in and just relax at home. What about you, do you have anything planned already?

q1.en: Not really anything concrete yet, but I definitely want to do something outdoors since the weather's supposed to be nice. Maybe I'll go hiking or just meet up with friends in the park.

a1.en: That sounds like a nice balance to the work week. Do you enjoy cooking on Sundays too, or do you usually order something instead?

q2.en: I really enjoy cooking on Sundays, usually something simple. It's become almost a little ritual for me. And what do you usually do when you really want to relax?

a2.en: I also love reading, ideally with a cup of coffee on the balcony when the sun's out. That's the perfect balance for me after a stressful week.

task.en:
Your new colleague starts today, but her password and her key for the workplace aren't ready yet.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Impression: What impression does a chaotic first day make?
IT department: How can the IT department help quickly?
Key: Could a borrowed key be a temporary solution?
Solution: How can the problem be resolved quickly?

q.en: We have a problem: our new colleague, Ms. Yilmaz, starts today, but her password for the computer hasn't been set up yet, and she hasn't received her key for the workplace either.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that on her first day she can get into neither the system nor the office properly?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what impression does that make on her if her first day starts off so chaotically?

a1.en: I think that's worse than we think - the first impression usually stays in someone's memory for a long time.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> call IT right away and ask for quick approval for a temporary password?

a2.en: That <r>certainly makes sense</r>, since otherwise she can't do anything all morning. I just hope it goes as quickly as it did last time.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to lend her my key temporarily, until reception has issued a new one for her.

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that you yourself won't be able to get into your own workplace anymore if you hand over your key.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> having reception lend us a spare key on short notice.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. The faster we sort this out, the more relaxed her first day can still become.

q5.en: In addition, we should also show her the org chart and the duty roster right away, so she gets an overview of the department.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. We could also explain the most important safety rules to her right away, before she settles into the open-plan office.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll take care of the password and the key, and you show her the building and the department. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to call IT already before the welcome?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we sort that out in the next ten minutes, before she arrives?

a7.en: That should be feasible, as long as IT reacts faster than we fear.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll organize the password and key right away, show her the org chart and the safety rules, so her first day still starts off well.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way she'll feel welcome from the start - after all, a good welcome culture is at least as important as the formalities themselves. I'll quickly let reception know and take care of it right away. <r>Let's also meet up with her briefly at lunch to hear how her first day is going so far.</r>

task.en:
A new colleague is very reserved and hardly takes part in conversations during breaks.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Cause: What could be the reason she doesn't feel integrated?
Common ground: How can a shared topic of conversation be found?
Approach: How can she be tactfully asked about her interests?
Time: How much time should be given for her to open up?

q.en: We have a problem: our new colleague, Ms. Berger, is very reserved and almost never joins the conversation during the coffee break. I think <g>it</g>'s hard for her to really feel comfortable with us.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that we haven't really integrated her into the team yet?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if she keeps feeling excluded like this?

a1.en: I think that at some point she'll distance herself internally from the team, even though her professional work is actually very good.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> try to find some common ground we could use to start a conversation with her?

a2.en: That <r>certainly makes sense</r>, since a shared topic often helps break the ice. Do you actually know what she's interested in?

q3.en: Another suggestion would be to just openly and tactfully ask her about her interests, without coming across as too pushy.

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that some people find it uncomfortable to be asked directly about personal things.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> first creating a relaxed, informal atmosphere, without immediately asking her anything personal.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. It's important to give her time, so she can open up on her own.

q5.en: In addition, we could actively invite her to our informal team activities, without putting too much pressure on her.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. There are surely small gestures that can establish a connection without making her uncomfortable.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: tomorrow I'll casually ask her about her free time during the break, and you invite her to have lunch together. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to do that already tomorrow morning?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we try that already during the first break?

a7.en: That should be feasible, as long as we really stay relaxed and open about it.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll create a relaxed atmosphere, tactfully ask her about shared interests, and invite her to informal activities, so she feels more comfortable on the team.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way we show her genuine interest without pressuring her - that should build a good connection in the long run. I'll talk to her about lunch first thing tomorrow. <r>Let's also touch base briefly on Friday to see how it went.</r>

task.en:
A colleague has received three new work assignments even though he already has two urgent deadlines.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What happens if he tries to do everything at once?
Priorities: How can the tasks be ordered by priority?
Delegation: Which tasks can be delegated to others?
Distribution: How can the work be divided sensibly?

q.en: We have a problem: Mr. Meier gave our colleague Lukas three new work assignments today, even though he already has two urgent deadlines by Friday. His workload is now simply too high.

a.en: <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the issue is that the priorities of the individual assignments aren't clear at all?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if Lukas tries to finish everything on time at the same time?

a1.en: I think that in the end nothing would really get finished properly, because he'd constantly have to jump back and forth between the tasks.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> talk to Mr. Meier and ask him to rank the new assignments by priority?

a2.en: That <r>certainly makes sense</r>, since then Lukas would at least know what needs to be done first. Do you know by when the new assignments are supposed to be done?

q3.en: Another suggestion would be for us to delegate some of the tasks to other colleagues who currently have less to do.

a3.en: <r>One argument against that is</r> that someone would first have to get familiar with an unfamiliar topic, which also costs time.

q4.en: <r>That's true, but</r> <r>we could perhaps solve the problem by</r> only delegating the simpler subtasks and letting Lukas handle the more complex assignments himself.

a4.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. That way responsibility stays clear, and the workload still gets noticeably smaller.

q5.en: In addition, we should ask Mr. Meier to give new instructions in writing rather than just verbally from now on, so nothing gets lost.

a5.en: <r>I think that's a good point</r>. Then we can also better check what's already done and what's still outstanding.

q6.en: Let's split up the tasks: I'll talk to Mr. Meier about the priorities, and you ask around the team who currently has capacity for additional tasks. Agreed?

a6.en: Agreed. Do you intend to have that conversation already today?

q7.en: Yes, would it be realistic if we sort that out before the team meeting?

a7.en: That should be feasible, as long as Mr. Meier still has time this afternoon.

q8.en: Let's summarize: we'll clarify the priorities with Mr. Meier, delegate the simpler subtasks, and ask for written instructions from now on, so Lukas's workload becomes manageable again.

a8.en: Exactly. I think that way Lukas keeps an overview <g>without</g> the deadlines being at risk. I'll note the key points in the minutes and send them to you right after the conversation. <r>Let's also get together briefly on Wednesday to check whether the new arrangement is working.</r>

task.en:
A new colleague is supposed to get trained in an important piece of software, but he's missing the login credentials, and a mentorship hasn't been officially arranged yet.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond to this situation.

These points can help you.
Consequences: What happens if the situation isn't resolved quickly?
Login credentials: How can the login credentials be obtained quickly?
Mentorship: Who could take on the mentorship?
Sharing: How can the mentorship be shared?

q.en: We have a problem: our new colleague, Mr. Fischer, is supposed to get trained in the data analysis software, but he's still missing the login credentials, and a mentorship <g>hasn't been officially set up</g> in his contract yet either.

a.en: <r>Ah, I see</r> - so that means he doesn't actually know who's supposed to train him or what he can even work with?

q1.en: Exactly. What do you think, what consequences would that have if we don't sort this out quickly?

a1.en: I think he'd feel pretty lost then and wouldn't really be able to use his first weeks productively.

q2.en: <r>How about we</r> contact IT right away and ask for the login credentials for the software?

a2.en: That <r>certainly makes sense</r>, since he can't practice at all without access. <r>I'm not entirely clear on</r> who's actually responsible for the approval, though.

q3.en: Another suggestion would be for me to become his mentor, since I'm most familiar with the software.
