q2.en: <r>That sounds good</r>. <r>What do you think if</r> we also actively inform all employees about their options, instead of them having to look into it themselves?

a2.en: <r>Yes, I think that's a good idea</r>. That way colleagues don't have to take care <g>of</g> the topic themselves, but get the information directly.

q3.en: True. And how do we make sure everyone actually ends up being treated equally?

a3.en: That's an excellent question. Maybe we could create a short checklist that gets applied consistently to every request.

q4.en: Good idea. And how do we best introduce the new rules to the team?

a4.en: <r>Maybe we could</r> present them at the next meeting and also base them on a few concrete examples.

q5.en: Good point. Should we work out the criteria this week, so we can get started quickly?

a5.en: Yes, that would make sense. I could write a first draft, if you take care of the examples.

q6.en: <r>Let's summarize</r>: we'll set clear criteria, actively inform everyone, create a checklist, and present it all at the next meeting.

a6.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I think that way we'll handle all requests fairly and consistently in the future.

task.en:
In your company, accidents and operating mistakes keep happening because new employees don't get the technical equipment in production properly explained to them. The existing manual is written in a very complicated way.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Explanation: How can you explain equipment more clearly?
Materials: What should a good manual include?
Onboarding: How can you better train new employees?
Safety: How do you make sure everyone operates the equipment safely?

q.en: <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: recently there have been several operating mistakes because new employees don't get the equipment in production properly explained to them.

a.en: I've heard about that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: the existing manual is simply written too complicated?

q1.en: Exactly, it's full of technical terms that are hard for new colleagues to understand. <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

a1.en: <r>I have an idea</r>: we could create a simpler quick-start guide with pictures showing the most important steps.

q2.en: <r>That sounds good</r>. <r>What do you think if</r> we also always have new employees try out the equipment under supervision first, before working with it alone?

a2.en: <r>Yes, I think that's a good idea</r>. That way experienced colleagues can show directly what each function is for.

q3.en: True. And how do we make sure safety doesn't get neglected in the process?

a3.en: That's an excellent question. Maybe we could highlight the most important safety instructions in color, so they stand out immediately.

q4.en: Good idea. And should we maybe also make a short briefing mandatory for all new employees?

a4.en: <r>Maybe we could</r> even combine that with a short practical test, before anyone works alone on a device.

q5.en: Good point. Should we finish the new quick-start guide this week, so we can get started soon?

a5.en: Yes, that would make sense. I could write the text, if you take care of the matching pictures.

q6.en: <r>Let's summarize</r>: we'll create a simple quick-start guide with pictures, introduce a briefing with practice, and clearly highlight the most important safety instructions.

a6.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I think that way new employees will understand the equipment much faster and more safely in the future.

task.en:
During an external quality inspection, several defects were found in the delivered products. The inspector said the error rate had risen significantly in recent months, and several customers had already complained.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Cause: What might be causing the error rate to rise?
Control: How can you improve quality control?
Communication: How do you inform the affected customers?
Prevention: How do you prevent similar problems in the future?

q.en: <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: during the external quality inspection, the inspector said the error rate <g>had risen</g> significantly in recent months.

a.en: I've heard about that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: several customers <g>had</g> already <g>complained</g> because of that?

q1.en: Exactly, he mentioned that too. <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

a1.en: <r>I have an idea</r>: we could first analyze exactly where in production most of the defects occur.

q2.en: <r>That sounds good</r>. <r>What do you think if</r> we also introduce a second quality check before shipping?

a2.en: <r>Yes, I think that's a good idea</r>. That way faulty products wouldn't even reach the customer in the first place.

q3.en: True. And how do we deal with the customers who have already complained?

a3.en: That's an excellent question. The inspector said many customers <g>would</g> mainly <g>expect</g> a quick response and a free replacement.

q4.en: Good idea. Should we then contact those customers directly and apologize?

a4.en: <r>Maybe we could</r> even do that today, then we'd show that we're taking the problem seriously.

q5.en: Good point. Should we introduce the new check this week, so we feel more confident again quickly?

a5.en: Yes, that would make sense. I could design the process for that, if you take care of the communication with the customers.

q6.en: <r>Let's summarize</r>: we'll analyze the sources of the defects, introduce a second quality check, and contact the affected customers today.

a6.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I think that way we'll win back the customers' trust and improve quality sustainably.

task.en:
Your colleague called in sick this morning and will be unable to work tomorrow's night shift. Next week's shift schedule is already very tight, and several colleagues have recently complained about short-notice cover arrangements.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Immediate solution: Who can step in at short notice?
Fairness: How can cover shifts be distributed fairly?
Long-term solution: Is a fixed stand-in plan needed?
Family-friendliness: How do you take colleagues with children into account?
Communication: How do you quickly inform the team about changes?

q.en: David, I need to tell you something quickly: Sabine called in sick this morning, so she won't be able to work tomorrow's night shift. <r>So we have the challenge that</r> we need to find someone for the shift by tomorrow morning. <r>How should we proceed</r>?

a.en: Oh no, that's really inconvenient. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so we don't have anyone for the night shift yet? Who do you think could step in at short notice?

q1.en: <r>I have an idea</r>: Thomas mentioned recently that he's flexible tomorrow afternoon. Maybe we could ask him if he can step in.

a1.en: <r>That's not a bad suggestion, but</r> Thomas has already covered for others twice in the past few weeks. I think we shouldn't keep putting the cover shifts on the same people.

q2.en: You're right. <r>Maybe we could solve the problem by</r> creating a list of volunteers for short-notice cover, where everyone can sign up voluntarily. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>That sounds convincing</r>. But we also need to remember that some colleagues with children can't always step in spontaneously. <r>I think it's better if</r> we combine the volunteer list with a fixed stand-in plan that takes family circumstances into account.

q3.en: Good point. We could also introduce a kind of on-call system – but only voluntary and with compensation, for example a day off later. <r>What do you think</r>?

a3.en: <r>I can only agree with that</r>. Compensation matters to me. Let's present the proposal at the next team meeting so everyone can have a say before we finalize anything.

q4.en: Good idea. We should also clarify how we quickly inform the whole team about short-notice changes – maybe through a shared chat group?

a4.en: <r>I think that's a very good idea</r>. A chat group would be practical, and we could also keep the shift schedule digital so everyone can check it anytime.

q5.en: <r>Then let's note down the following points</r>: for tomorrow we'll ask Thomas if he can step in, and we'll also prepare the proposal for the volunteer list, stand-in plan and chat group for the team meeting.

a5.en: <r>Agreed, that's a good solution</r>. I'll take care of the written summary, and you have a quick word with Thomas about tomorrow.

task.en:
Management has noticed that the sickness rate in the team has risen noticeably over the past few months. Several colleagues complain of back pain and exhaustion, and absences keep increasing.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Cause: Why has the sickness rate probably risen?
Workstation: How can the screen workstation be made more ergonomic?
Exercise and relaxation: What offerings for sports and stress management would make sense?
Nutrition: How can the canteen contribute to a healthier offering?
Next steps: How and when do you present the proposals to management?

q.en: Nina, do you have a moment? <r>We have the challenge that</r> the sickness rate in the team has risen noticeably in the last few months. After <g>analyzing</g> the sick notes, I mainly see back pain and exhaustion as the main causes.

a.en: I noticed that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so the absences are mainly related to back pain and exhaustion? <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: through the <g>improvement</g> of ergonomics at the screen workstations, we could probably reduce the back pain. Height-adjustable desks would be one option, for example.

a1.en: <r>That sounds reasonable</r>, but I don't think that alone is enough. The workload is simply too high, and many people barely manage to take breaks at all.

q2.en: <r>You're right about that</r>. <r>How about</r> we introduce a fixed break schedule and also offer a fitness programme with relaxation exercises? <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. But we mustn't forget that not everyone feels like doing sports. Maybe we could also offer a prevention seminar on stress management.

q3.en: Good addition. And what about food? I've heard that a lot of people complain about the canteen food.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you</r>. <r>One option would be, for example,</r> to develop a balanced range and a sustainable meal plan with the canteen, with more fresh vegetables and fewer ready meals.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: through the <g>introduction</g> of a fitness programme, a fixed break schedule, a prevention seminar, and a healthier canteen offering, we want to bring the sickness rate down.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll talk to the canteen about the meal plan, and you take care of the offer for the fitness programme and the seminar.

q5.en: Should we also present the whole thing to management before we start?

a5.en: Good idea. We'll briefly summarize the proposals and present them at next week's meeting, then we can start implementing right away.

task.en:
At the last team meeting, several colleagues criticized that the internal short presentations are often hard to follow – they lack structure, clear transitions, and a recognizable key message.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Problem: Why are the short presentations hard to follow?
Structure: How should a good short presentation be structured?
Tools: What stock phrases and aids (e.g., diagrams) could help?
Preparation: How can colleagues prepare better?
Implementation: How and when do you introduce the new rules?

q.en: Alex, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: at the last team meeting, several colleagues said that our short presentations are often hard to follow.

a.en: I've heard that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so <g>it</g>'s mainly about the structure of the talks? <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: <r>From my point of view, an argument for that is that</r> a clear introduction is often missing, and many people dive straight into the topic <g>without</g> saying what it's actually about.

a1.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. In my experience it also helps a lot if you highlight the key message again at the end. That's particularly important to me, because otherwise listeners often don't know what they're actually supposed to take away.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: we could create a short checklist – with fixed phrases for the introduction, for moving on to a new point, and for the conclusion. I prefer as short a version as possible, one people can memorize quickly. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. But we mustn't forget that a talk also becomes much clearer with a suitable diagram. We could also show a concrete example for that.

q3.en: Good point. For one thing, we could add example sentences to the checklist; for another, we could briefly get feedback from a colleague before the talk.

a3.en: Good point, however we shouldn't make the whole thing too complicated, otherwise nobody will feel like giving a talk at all in the end. For me, practicality is the decisive factor.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: we'll create a simple checklist with phrases for the introduction, main part, and conclusion, plus an example with a diagram, and we'll offer brief feedback before the talk.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll take care of the checklist, and you put together the example with the diagram.

q5.en: Should we also present this briefly to the colleagues at the next meeting?

a5.en: Good idea. That way everyone will immediately know what matters, and we can try out the checklist starting with the next short presentation.

task.en:
In recent weeks there have been several misunderstandings in the team because chat messages were often phrased very directly or unclearly. This has noticeably strained the mood in the team.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Cause: Why do the misunderstandings arise?
Communication method: When should you talk in person rather than in writing?
Language: How can messages be phrased more politely?
Rules: What rules could help (e.g., letting others finish, asking follow-up questions)?
Implementation: How do you introduce the new rules to the team?

q.en: David, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: I've noticed that there have been several misunderstandings in the team lately, because chat messages were often phrased very directly or unclearly.

a.en: True, I've <g>actually</g> noticed that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so it's mainly about the tone in our written communication?

q1.en: Exactly. Julia found a message pretty blunt last week, even though it certainly wasn't meant that way. In chat, people just write quickly without thinking about the tone.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. Maybe we should think about when a chat message actually makes sense and when it's better to just stop by or call instead.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: we could, <g>after all</g>, agree that important or sensitive topics should generally be clarified in conversation, not just in writing. That way you at least see the body language and can clear up misunderstandings right away. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. We should also get into the habit of letting the other person finish first and asking follow-up questions before questioning or criticizing something.

q3.en: Good point. And when writing, we could try to phrase things more politely instead of saying directly what bothers us – so not beating around the bush, but also not too blunt.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. How should we actually communicate that to the team without it sounding like a lecture?

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: we'll agree to clarify sensitive topics in person, let others finish speaking, and phrase messages more politely. We'll present that briefly at the next meeting.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll summarize the points briefly, and you bring it up at the meeting.

q5.en: Do you think that's enough to improve the mood in the team again?

a5.en: It'll work out <g>just fine</g> if everyone pays a bit more attention to their tone. The conversational atmosphere will definitely improve.

task.en:
A colleague has repeatedly missed important deadlines recently, and project handovers were incomplete. The team can no longer really rely on him, and a clarifying performance conversation is coming up.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Problem: What exactly is the problem?
Preparation: How do you prepare for the conversation objectively?
Conducting the conversation: How do you address the problem without embarrassing anyone?
Proposed solutions: What concrete solutions could you suggest?
Follow-up: How do you make sure the situation doesn't happen again?

q.en: Julia, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: I need to have a conversation with Tom soon, because he's missed several important deadlines recently and the handovers were incomplete.

a.en: I've noticed that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so <g>it</g>'s mainly about his unreliability with project handovers? <r>What could you do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: Exactly. The problem is that the team can no longer really rely on him, and that already worries me because of the impact on the other projects.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. But it's important that you handle the conversation objectively and don't embarrass him in front of others. <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: use I-statements instead, for example „I've noticed that…“ rather than „You always…“.

q2.en: Good point. And I should probably also try to see it from his perspective – maybe there's another issue behind it. <r>What do you think</r> if I just start by asking how he's doing?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. That way you immediately show that it's not only about criticism. After that, you could specifically address which deadlines were affected and what impact that had.

q3.en: And in the end we should probably look for solutions together, right? For example, more transparency in calculating deadlines, so it's clear how much time is realistically needed.

a3.en: <r>I completely agree with you</r>. You could also agree that he lets you know early if there's a problem, <g>instead of</g> just letting the deadline pass. That would help prevent conflicts in the future.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let me summarize</r>: I'll first ask about his situation, address the deadlines objectively using I-statements, and suggest more transparency plus early feedback as a solution.

a4.en: Exactly, that's the best way to do it. If you want, I can practice the wording with you beforehand.

q5.en: That would be great. And what do I do if he simply denies the problem?

a5.en: Then stay calm and factual and give concrete examples – that's hard to argue with. In the end, what matters most is that you find a solution together.

task.en:
Management wants to introduce more automated processes and AI-supported tools, but there is uncertainty and concern about job security within the team.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Benefit: What benefits could automation bring?
Concerns: What concerns do colleagues have?
Security: How do you ensure data protection and cybersecurity?
Rollout: How do you introduce the new tools step by step?
Support: What training or support do employees need?

q.en: Alex, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: management wants to introduce more automated processes and AI-supported tools, but there are some concerns in the team.

a.en: I've heard that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so it's mainly about uncertainty regarding automation? <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: Exactly. Some people are worried that the newly <g>introduced</g> tools will completely take over their tasks and that jobs could disappear.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. It would be important to clearly communicate that automation is mainly meant to take over repetitive tasks, so there's more time for more demanding work.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: we could start a small pilot project, for example with the rapidly <g>growing</g> number of customer service requests, and then show the results transparently. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. But we should also keep cybersecurity in mind – for example through encryption, regular backups, and two-factor authentication, so that no data protection issues arise.

q3.en: Good point. And we could present the well <g>documented</g> results of the pilot project at the next meeting, so everyone can see what's actually improving.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. We should also offer training so everyone feels confident using the new digital tools.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: we'll start a pilot project in customer service, pay attention to data protection and cybersecurity, document the results, and offer suitable training.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll take care of the technical side, and you talk to management about the training.

q5.en: Should we also keep the team regularly informed about the progress?

a5.en: Definitely. That keeps everything transparent, and the colleagues who were initially skeptical will see that their concerns are being taken seriously.

task.en:
A colleague is considering going self-employed and building his own consulting business with international clients. However, he's unsure whether he can afford it financially and how best to prepare for this step.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Finances: What financial questions does he need to clarify beforehand?
Coverage: What about health and unemployment insurance?
Target market: How do you find a suitable international target market?
Risks: What risks should be considered (competition, language barriers)?
Decision: How do you prepare a well-thought-out decision?

q.en: Mark, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: David is thinking about going self-employed and building his own consulting business with international clients, but he's totally unsure.

a.en: He's told me that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so <g>it</g>'s mainly about the financial side? <r>What could we advise him in this situation</r>?

q1.en: Exactly. He's wondering whether he can even afford it financially if he gives up his secure job and protection against dismissal.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. He should take a close look beforehand at how health insurance and unemployment insurance would work – as a self-employed person, you usually have to sort that out yourself.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: he could set aside a financial buffer for six to twelve months before quitting. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. He should also think about which target market he actually wants to address – especially with international clients, language barriers and cultural differences play a role too.

q3.en: Good point. And he should also look at the competition in his industry, so he knows how to stay competitive.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. Maybe he could also talk to the chamber of commerce – they often offer free advice on such questions.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: he should build a financial buffer, sort out his insurance, choose a suitable target market, and get advice from the chamber of commerce.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what I'd suggest to him too. I'm happy to send him the chamber of commerce's contact details.

q5.en: That would be great. Do you think we should also tell him about someone who's already done this?

a5.en: Definitely. A personal conversation with someone who's already self-employed usually helps more than any checklist.

task.en:
Due to the new supply chain due diligence act, the company has to produce a detailed sustainability report starting next year. So far no one on the team has dealt with CSR topics, and the deadline is approaching.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Problem: Why is this a problem for the team?
Responsibility: Who could specialize in this topic?
Timeline: How can this be achieved within the deadline?
Support: What training or external help would make sense?
Future: What new tasks or jobs could emerge from this?

q.en: Alex, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: <g>due to</g> the new supply chain due diligence act, our company has to produce a detailed sustainability report starting next year, and so far no one here has dealt with CSR topics.

a.en: I've noticed that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so it's mainly about a lack of expertise in the team? <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: Exactly. And the deadline is getting closer – we'd need to prepare the first report <g>within</g> the next six months.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. Maybe we should ask someone on the team whether they'd like to specialize in sustainability, instead of hiring completely new people.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: we could look for a suitable training course and then also offer that person new promotion prospects as a CSR officer. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. We should also check whether we should bring in external support, for example a consultant who can guide us through the first report.

q3.en: Good point. And <g>despite</g> the tight schedule, we should also start dealing with topics like diversity and accessibility right away, since that's also part of the reporting obligation.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. That could even lead to a whole new position in the company in the long run – jobs like that are becoming increasingly important.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: we'll look for someone on the team for training in sustainability, bring in external support if needed, and take care of diversity and accessibility in good time.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll ask around the team who'd be interested in specializing.

q5.en: Do you think management will support this?

a5.en: Definitely, especially if we show that it could also create new career opportunities for the team in the long run.

task.en:
The company wants to switch to agile working with Scrum and introduce flatter hierarchies starting next quarter. Several colleagues are unsure because they seem to be lacking important future skills.

Discuss with your conversation partner how you would respond appropriately to this situation.

These points can help you.
Problem: Why are some colleagues unsure?
Skills: What future skills does the team specifically need?
Training: How can you develop these skills in a targeted way?
Practice: How can you try out the new way of working step by step?
Support: Who could support the team through this?

q.en: Anna, do you have a moment? <r>We should talk about a problem</r>: starting next quarter, the company wants to switch to agile working with Scrum, but several colleagues are quite unsure about it.

a.en: I've heard that too. <r>Did I understand you correctly</r>: so <g>it</g>'s mainly about a lack of experience with the new way of working? <r>What could we do in this situation</r>?

q1.en: Exactly. Many feel like they're missing important future skills – for example agility, negotiation skills, or working with data analysis.

a1.en: <r>I can understand that</r>. You don't learn that overnight, after all. Maybe we should first find out what skills already exist in the team and where exactly the gaps are.

q2.en: <r>I'd have a suggestion</r>: we could offer a short training course on Scrum and Kanban before we actually switch over. <r>What do you think</r>?

a2.en: <r>I like that</r>. In addition, we could first test a sprint with a small pilot team, so everyone can try out in practice how agile working actually works.

q3.en: Good point. And maybe someone with experience, for example from a startup, could support the team at the start and answer questions.

a3.en: <r>I agree with you on that</r>. That would take some of the pressure off colleagues and definitely make the cultural shift toward flatter hierarchies easier.

q4.en: <r>Alright, let's summarize</r>: we'll first identify the skill gaps, offer training on Scrum and Kanban, test the new way of working with a pilot team, and get experienced support.

a4.en: Exactly, that's what we'll do. I'll ask around in our network who might work as a mentor.

q5.en: Do you think that's enough to make everyone in the team feel more confident?

a5.en: Definitely, especially if we show that continuous training is possible here and that you really never stop learning.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I think introducing more home-office days is a good idea.

explanation.en:
„Einerseits“ opens a two-sided argument („Einerseits“ … Andererseits).
„Außerdem“ only adds information, it does not prepare a counterargument.
„Deshalb“ expresses a consequence, not a weighing.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I am of the opinion that flexible working hours increase productivity.

explanation.en:
„Grundsätzlich“ signals a general, fundamental position.
„Einerseits“ expects an „Andererseits“.
„Im Großen und Ganzen“ summarises what has already been said.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I advocate for an extension of parental leave.

explanation.en:
„Ausdrücklich“ emphasises clarity and determination.
„Selbstverständlich“ sounds too self-evident.
„Im Übrigen“ introduces an additional point, not a stance.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} rising energy costs, many households are heavily burdened.

explanation.en:
„Aufgrund + Genitiv“ is most common in formal written German.
„In exam contexts it is preferred over the more colloquial „Wegen“.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I would like to emphasise that further training is an important factor.

explanation.en:
„In diesem Zusammenhang“ refers to the thematic context of what preceded.
„An dieser Stelle“ is spatial / temporal.
„Darüber hinaus“ adds information but does not link to the context.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} current developments, action is required.

explanation.en:
„Angesichts + Genitiv“ means „in view of, considering“.
„Aufgrund“ would be causal.
„Hinsichtlich“ means „regarding X“ — thematic, not evaluative.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} there are also people who find online meetings less effective.

explanation.en:
„Andererseits“ is the classic counterpart to „Einerseits“ introducing the counterargument.
„Außerdem“ would only add.
„Daher / Folglich“ are consequence connectors.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the advantages, the high financial burden remains a serious problem.

explanation.en:
„Trotz + Genitiv“ expresses concession.
„Wegen / Aufgrund“ are causal.
„Angesichts“ relates to consideration, not contrast.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} it cannot be denied that the reform also carries risks.

explanation.en:
„Dennoch“ introduces a concessive statement.
„Trotzdem“ is more colloquial.
„Allerdings“ restricts but without as strong a contrast.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the measure is controversial because it may lead to more bureaucracy.

explanation.en:
„Allerdings“ restricts a previous positive statement.
„Hingegen“ directly contrasts two things.
„Allerdings“ sounds more balanced and is more common in exam German.

sentence.en: Some support the measure — {{BLANK}} see it as a restriction.

explanation.en:
„andere hingegen“ is the set paired formula: Manche … andere hingegen.
„andere jedoch“ is grammatically correct but less idiomatic.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the positive aspects, the disadvantages must not be ignored.

explanation.en:
„Neben + Dativ“ means „in addition to“.
„Trotz“ expresses concession.
„Außer“ means exclusion.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} it is important that companies invest more in sustainability.

explanation.en:
All four express personal opinion. In DTB B2, „Meiner Meinung nach“ and
„Meiner Ansicht nach“ are tested most often. Pay attention to correct word order.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} this argument convinces me because it is based on facts.

explanation.en:
„Persönlich“ emphasises the individual stance.
„Grundsätzlich“ is too general.
„Eigentlich“ would have a concessive nuance.
„Ehrlich gesagt“ is more colloquial.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I consider the proposed solution to be sensible.

explanation.en:
„Insgesamt“ sums up a balanced consideration.
„Im Großen und Ganzen“ is very similar but longer.
„Letztendlich“ focuses on the outcome.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I have come to the conclusion that digital education is forward-looking.

explanation.en:
„Letztendlich“ expresses a final personal judgement.
„Schließlich“ can be temporal.
„Insgesamt“ summarises but does not conclude with a personal verdict.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} your job advertisement of 15 March I hereby apply for the advertised position.

explanation.en:
„Auf + Akkusativ“ is the set phrasing for applications: „Auf Ihre Ausschreibung …“.
„Bezüglich / Hinsichtlich“ are correct but less idiomatic for cover letters.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} your advertisement in the Süddeutsche Zeitung I am writing to you.

explanation.en:
„Bezugnehmend auf“ is the classic opening for formal correspondence.
„In Bezug auf“ is equivalent but less elegant at the start of a letter.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} your letter of 3 March I inform you that we accept your offer.

explanation.en:
„In Antwort auf“ is the formal letter formula for a reply.
„Als Antwort auf“ is more colloquial.
„Betreffend“ introduces a topic, not a reply.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I have carefully reviewed your offer and would now like to respond.

explanation.en:
„Mit großem Interesse“ is a set formula for positive business correspondence.
„Mit Interesse“ is shorter but less emphatic.
„Mit Freude“ sounds too personal.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I refer to our telephone conversation of yesterday.

explanation.en:
„Hiermit“ is a typical opening word in German business letters — it refers to the current act of writing.
„Somit / Damit / Deshalb“ are consequence connectors.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I am happy to be available for any queries.

explanation.en:
„Bei Bedarf“ is the idiomatic letter formula.
„Im Bedarfsfall“ is a slight synonym but rarer. In an exam context „Bei Bedarf“ is the safest choice.

sentence.en: I {{BLANK}} ask you to send me the documents as soon as possible.

explanation.en:
„Ich würde Sie bitten“ is the formal Konjunktiv II for polite requests.
„Ich möchte bitten“ is more colloquial. Konjunktiv II signals politeness.

sentence.en: For any queries I am happy to {{BLANK}} at your disposal.

explanation.en:
„Zur Verfügung stehen“ is the set phrase for readiness to help.
„Zur Verfügung sein“ does not exist.
„Zur Verfügung halten“ means to keep something ready.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} present our new offer to you.

explanation.en:
„Wir erlauben uns“ is a standardised polite formula.
„Wir gestatten uns“ is a synonym but rarer in modern business German.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} your positive response we are very pleased.

explanation.en:
„Sich freuen + über + Akkusativ“ is the correct prepositional government.
„Sich freuen + auf + Akkusativ“ would be for future events. Here it refers to the result.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} inform you that your order has been received.

explanation.en:
„Hiermit“ refers to the act of writing itself.
„Somit / Folglich“ are logical conclusions.
„Demnach“ means „accordingly“.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} you to settle the invoice within 14 days.

explanation.en:
„Wir bitten Sie“ is the standard polite phrasing.
„Ersuchen“ is more formal, common in official language.
„Fordern / Verlangen“ sound too authoritative.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} our previous cooperation we look forward to further collaboration.

explanation.en:
„Aufgrund“ expresses causality.
„Dank“ would also be positive and possible.
„Angesichts“ is more for critical situations.
„Infolge“ emphasises consequences, not motivations.

sentence.en: We are {{BLANK}} to present you with a special offer.

explanation.en:
„In der Lage sein“ is the formal expression for ability.
„Imstande sein“ is a direct synonym but „in der Lage“ is more frequent in written German.

sentence.en: Please let us know {{BLANK}} whether you are interested in our offer.

explanation.en:
„Baldmöglichst“ is the classic expression in business German.
„Zeitnah“ is modern and acceptable.
„Umgehend“ sounds more urgent.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} a confirmation from your side.

explanation.en:
„Würden uns freuen“ (Konjunktiv II) is the polite letter formula.
„Freuen uns“ would be Indicative — too direct. Konjunktiv II signals politeness.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the costs are high, the investment pays off in the long term.

explanation.en:
All four are concessive. „Obwohl“ + subordinate clause is most common.
„Obgleich / Wenngleich“ are archaic. In DTB B2 „Obwohl“ is the safest choice.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} all criticism, the project proved to be a success.

explanation.en:
„Trotz + Genitiv“ expresses concession: despite the criticism being present.
„Wegen / Aufgrund“ are causal.
„Angesichts“ is for confrontation, less for a positive result.

sentence.en: I understand your concerns, {{BLANK}} I would still like to advocate for my position.

explanation.en:
„Jedoch“ introduces the contrasting clause without being as strong as „Dennoch“.
„Trotzdem“ is more colloquial.
„Allerdings“ restricts the previous statement.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I understand the criticism, I do not share it entirely.

explanation.en: „Auch wenn“ + Indicative is correct here — one concedes understanding the criticism but does not share it. In exam contexts check whether Konjunktiv or Indicative follows.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the previous year, turnover has doubled.

explanation.en:
„Im Vergleich zu“ is the most neutral comparative expression.
„Im Gegensatz zu“ emphasises the contrast more.
„Gegenüber“ is shorter and also correct.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} the old method, the new one is significantly more efficient.

explanation.en:
„Im Gegensatz zu“ emphasises the contradiction / contrast.
„Im Vergleich zu“ is more neutral.
„Statt“ means replacement, not contrast.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} it can be said that the measure was successful.

explanation.en:
„Zusammenfassend“ introduces a conclusion.
„Abschließend“ relates to the close of a speech.
„Insgesamt“ is a summary word but not a typical sentence opener.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} we can note that demand has increased.

explanation.en:
„Abschließend“ signals the last point in an argument.
„Zusammenfassend“ summarises several points.
„Daher / Folglich“ express causal consequence.

sentence.en: The noise level is too high, {{BLANK}} we should take action.

explanation.en: All five adverbs express a consequence. „Daher“ differs stylistically, as it sounds more formal and elegant in standard written German than the more colloquial „deshalb“ or „deswegen“.

sentence.en: The project has failed, {{BLANK}} we must seek new approaches.

explanation.en:
„Folglich“ emphasises the logical conclusion.
„Infolgedessen“ is correct but more formal and longer.
„Daher“ is a direct synonym
both are suitable for the exam.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} rising demand the company has expanded its production.

explanation.en:
„Infolge + Genitiv“ expresses direct consequential causality.
„Aufgrund“ is similar but more general.
„Dank“ has a positive connotation.
„Angesichts“ is for confrontation.

sentence.en: The survey shows that it is {{BLANK}} to drive digitalisation forward.

explanation.en: „Dringend erforderlich“ is the standardised expression in business German for necessary measures. The other variants are stylistically less precise.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} your job advertisement of 1 April I apply for the position.

explanation.en:
„Bezugnehmend auf“ is the classic formal opening for job applications.
„Auf“ is shorter and also idiomatic. Both are accepted in exam contexts.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} it must be admitted that the old solutions have limitations.

explanation.en:
„Auch wenn“ expresses concessive hypotheses.
„Obwohl“ does not require Konjunktiv.
„Selbst wenn“ is more emphatic.
„Trotzdem“ is a sentence adverb, not a subjunctor.

sentence.en: We {{BLANK}} your reply by 30 June.

explanation.en:
„Entgegensehen“ (+ Dative) is the set formula: „Wir sehen Ihrer Antwort entgegen.“
„Erwarten“ would also be grammatical but less formally idiomatic in letter closings.

sentence.en: {{BLANK}} I share the view that more investment is needed.

explanation.en:
„Vollständig teile ich“ means complete agreement.
„Weitgehend“ would be partial agreement.
„Grundsätzlich“ is correct but weaker.

topic.en: New location

task.en: All employees are expected to move or commute, as your company is opening a new location. The location is equipped with state-of-the-art technology, but is 75 km from the current site.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management wants to relocate our company's site. All employees are expected to either move or commute.
<r>I don't think this idea is good.</r> Although this situation offers us many opportunities, it makes our everyday work life very complicated.
<r>On the one hand</r>, the new site has state-of-the-art technology, which has a positive effect on our company. There we can gain new experience, take further training and build a career.

<r>On the other hand</r>, we lose a lot of time if we have to commute two hours to work every day. Many employees have families and want to spend their free time with their children. In addition, the high travel costs are an argument against commuting. Moreover, moving would be very difficult for families with children, since the children would have to change kindergarten or school.

<r>That's why I suggest that</r> employees be able to choose between working from home and commuting. This way, employees could work one week at the company and one week at home, which would save travel costs and time.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinions.</r>
Anna

topic.en: Sustainable business trips

task.en: For environmental reasons, business trips under 800 kilometers are to take place only by train instead of by plane in future. The train journey often takes significantly longer than the flight.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to have business trips under 800 kilometers carried out only by train in the future. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this policy basically makes sense, even if it won't always be easy to implement in everyday life.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> the reduction of our CO2 emissions, since trains are much more environmentally friendly than planes. In addition, travel time can often be used productively to prepare for appointments.
<r>On the other hand</r>, a longer journey also means less time for our actual work. In the case of short-notice appointments, a delayed train could also lead to serious problems.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> we allow exceptions in the implementation, when a train journey is really not an option for time reasons.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Julia

topic.en: Company sports during working hours

task.en: Management wants to introduce a weekly fitness program that all employees are expected to attend during working hours, in order to strengthen health promotion in the workplace.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning a weekly fitness program for all employees. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> introducing such a program basically makes sense, even if the concrete implementation won't be equally easy for every department.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> stress relief: company sports during working hours promote movement and demonstrably improve the ability to concentrate. In addition, a regular fitness program can lower the sickness rate in the long term.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one hour of company sports per week also means one hour less for actual work, which could increase the workload elsewhere. Moreover, not all colleagues have the same physical fitness, so a mandatory program would overwhelm rather than relieve some of them.

<r>That's why I suggest that</r> participation in the fitness program remain voluntary, and that other forms of health promotion be offered instead, such as ergonomic screen workstations or better break arrangements.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Mark

topic.en: Support program for foreign professional qualifications

task.en: Management wants to introduce an internal support program: new employees with a foreign professional qualification are to be temporarily assigned to a different department during the recognition procedure, until their qualification is officially recognized.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning a new support program: colleagues with a foreign professional qualification are to be temporarily assigned to a different department during the recognition procedure. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this support was long overdue – especially for everyone whose qualification is not yet recognized here.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that those affected wouldn't simply have to wait during the often lengthy recognition process, but could already gain practical experience and specialize in a new department – for example in the IT department or in logistics.

<r>On the other hand</r>, a temporary assignment to an unfamiliar department isn't easy for everyone: anyone who has submitted an application for recognition of their professional qualification often already has to submit numerous documents from their country of origin, and as long as the application hasn't been processed yet, the additional adjustment at work could unsettle some people rather than relieve them.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> every affected person be assigned a fixed contact person who provides advice and is immediately responsible for questions about the procedure.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Nina

topic.en: Approval requirement for side jobs

task.en: Management wants to introduce a rule that every side job must be approved in writing in advance, in order to avoid possible overlaps with the main position according to the collective agreement.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning that every side job will have to be approved in advance in the future. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this policy is understandable, even if it means extra effort for some colleagues.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that this way both the employees' work-life balance and compliance with the collective agreement are kept in view. Anyone already under time pressure is thus protected from taking on too much responsibility.

<r>On the other hand</r>, for many a side job is not only a financial necessity but also a chance to gain qualifications in another field. An additional approval requirement could discourage some people rather than support them.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> approval only be required in the case of an actual overlap with the main position, and not generally for every side job.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
David

topic.en: 360-degree feedback on our key qualifications

task.en: Management wants to introduce an annual 360-degree feedback: colleagues are to assess each other on key qualifications such as teamwork skills, communication skills and resilience.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning an annual 360-degree feedback on our key qualifications. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> such feedback on qualities like reliability or willingness to learn can basically be helpful, even though it should be no substitute for a personal conversation with one's manager.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that we find out more honestly how our teamwork skills, our communication skills, our initiative or our resilience are perceived by colleagues – aspects that one often can't assess in oneself at all.

<r>On the other hand</r>, anonymous feedback isn't always constructive: some comments could be unfair or not comprehensible at all and could even harm the working atmosphere, if no one has to justify the criticism in more detail.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> every comment has to be briefly justified in writing, so that no assessment is given without a concrete example.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Alex

topic.en: Internal job posting before external search

task.en: Management wants to introduce a rule that every open position is first posted internally for two weeks before an external job ad is published on job portals.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning that every open position will first be posted internally for two weeks in the future, before it is published externally on job portals. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this policy is fair, because it gives all colleagues the same chance to apply for a new position.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that both our experience in the company and our knowledge of internal processes are finally given greater consideration. The earlier one applies internally, the greater the chances of really being heard.

<r>On the other hand</r>, not every position is interesting for internal colleagues, and anyone who has been waiting a long time for a certain position could still end up empty-handed if the requirements match neither their own experience nor their desired development.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> the internal posting not only be visible online on the intranet, but also actively mentioned in team meetings, in order to really reach everyone.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Julia

topic.en: Updated CV for internal job changes

task.en: Management wants to introduce a rule that all employees must submit an updated tabular CV with details of their career history, education, and IT and language skills whenever they change positions within the company.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning that an updated CV will have to be submitted for every internal job change in the future. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this update basically makes sense, because an outdated CV with incorrect information about one's education or language skills doesn't look very serious.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that HR always has a well-maintained overview of our career history, our qualifications and our IT skills – which saves a lot of time especially for internal applications. Besides, we then also become responsible for our own information ourselves.

<r>On the other hand</r>, some colleagues hardly ever need to update their CV, because nothing changes about their job for years. Nevertheless, everyone is apparently supposed to do the same task regularly, which doesn't seem very consistent.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> we make it easier for ourselves and in future only have to update the relevant information about our current qualification or new language skills.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Anna

topic.en: In-house apprenticeships instead of external specialists

task.en: Management wants to train more of its own apprentices through dual vocational training in the future, instead of hiring already qualified specialists from outside.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to train more of its own apprentices in the future, instead of hiring ready-made specialists. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this decision is wise in the long run, even though a dual apprenticeship requires more time and supervision at the beginning than hiring ready-made specialists.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that we can train apprentices according to our own standards from the very beginning, without having to retrain them extensively later. Anyone who finishes vocational school with good grades also often already has realistic chances of being taken on during the apprenticeship.

<r>On the other hand</r>, a dual apprenticeship costs the company time and money over several years, and not every apprentice actually stays with the company in the end. The longer the training takes, the greater the risk also becomes that well-trained apprentices will switch to a different employer after completing it.

<r>That's why I suggest that</r> we make more of an effort to stay in contact with vocational schools, in order to promote our training company early on, instead of only considering who will be taken on shortly before the end of the apprenticeship.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Nina

topic.en: Uniform onboarding program for all new employees

task.en: Management wants to introduce a uniform onboarding program: all new employees – whether in a permanent position, on a fixed-term contract or as an intern – are to go through the same structured induction phase with fixed training measures in the future.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning a uniform onboarding program for all new employees. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this idea is basically good, even though a uniform induction phase won't be equally useful for every position.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that new employees receive the same basics from the very beginning during the induction phase, and thus find their way around the company more quickly. By planning fixed training measures, we also ensure a consistent quality of induction.

<r>On the other hand</r>, a uniform program quickly makes experienced career-changers feel as if they didn't know anything about working life yet. Anyone who already brings years of professional experience probably hardly needs the same detailed introduction as an intern without prior knowledge.

HR does point out that the program is said to be equally useful for everyone. <r>That's why I suggest that</r> they nevertheless adapt it individually according to prior experience, instead of prescribing the same induction phase for everyone.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
David

topic.en: Switch to an open-plan office

task.en: Management wants to abolish all individual offices and instead set up a single open-plan office in which all employees share a common work area.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to abolish all individual offices and set up one large open-plan office instead. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this change is well-intentioned, even though workplace ergonomics can't be considered equally well for everyone in the process.

<r>One advantage would undoubtedly be</r> that we can exchange ideas more quickly in the open-plan office and spontaneous meetings become much easier. The more open the space is designed, the easier collaboration between departments becomes for us.

<r>On the other hand</r>, the noise level in an open-plan office usually also rises significantly, and not everyone feels equally comfortable there. Especially for concentrated work, we then often lack a quiet retreat.

<r>That's why I suggest that</r> management not make this decision alone, but ask us again beforehand. That way, in addition to the open-plan office, some smaller retreat rooms for concentrated work or confidential conversations could also be kept.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Alex

topic.en: Buddy program for new colleagues

task.en: Management wants to introduce a buddy program: every new employee is to be given a fixed contact person from the team during the first weeks, who helps with getting started.

parts.en: Hello everyone,
<r>as you have probably already heard, management is planning</r> to introduce a buddy program for new employees. <r>I would also like to write something about this in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> it is often difficult for new colleagues at the beginning to break the ice and find a familiar atmosphere in the team.

<r>One advantage would certainly be</r> that getting to know each other would become much easier with a fixed contact person, and the first contact with the team would be much more pleasant. In addition, the buddy could help with small talk during breaks and thus show genuine interest in the new colleague.

<r>On the other hand</r>, not all colleagues have enough time to additionally take care of a new person without their own work suffering. Moreover, not every buddy automatically matches the character of the new employee, which could make the conversation feel rather formal instead of relaxed at first.

<r>That's why I suggest that</r> the buddy and the new colleague be briefly asked in advance, so that they are a good match for each other and the conversation goes smoothly, openly and tactfully from the start.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Mark

topic.en: New tool for assigning work tasks

task.en: Management wants to introduce a digital tool with which all work tasks will in future be assigned in writing, given a deadline and priority, and documented. Until now, many tasks were delegated only verbally in passing.

parts.en: To everyone,
<r>as you probably already know, management wants</r> to introduce a new tool for work tasks. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this idea makes sense, because verbal instructions often lead to misunderstandings.

<r>One advantage would certainly be</r> that responsibility for each task is clearly documented, and in case of queries we immediately know who is responsible for what. In addition, we then see the priority and deadline at a glance.

<r>On the other hand</r>, the additional documentation takes up time that we then lack for the actual work. Moreover, some colleagues fear that spontaneous, short arrangements would become more complicated as a result.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> we use the tool only for larger or urgent tasks and that we may continue to clarify smaller arrangements verbally, as long as they are briefly noted in the log.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Julia

topic.en: Mandatory certification for hard skills

task.en: Management is planning that employees will in future have to prove certification in at least one hard-skill area, such as data analysis, digital transformation or labour law, every two years.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you have probably already heard, management is planning</r> to introduce mandatory certification for hard skills. <r>I would also like to write something about this in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> whoever regularly refreshes their knowledge benefits from it in the long run, even if an obligation may seem unpleasant at first.

<r>One advantage would certainly be</r> that this would let us keep pace with digital transformation and apply our skills without losing touch. In addition, whoever can present a certification often has better chances with internal applications.

<r>On the other hand</r>, management should consider that not every department needs the same hard skills, and whoever works in occupational safety, for example, hardly needs certification in market research. Moreover, the courses would have to take place during working hours, otherwise the burden would become too great.
<r>That's why I suggest that</r> each department determine for itself which hard skills are really relevant, and that certification remain voluntary but be supported financially and in terms of time.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Anna

topic.en: New meeting rules – more structure for meetings

task.en: Management wants to introduce fixed meeting rules in future, such as a mandatory agenda and a limited speaking time for each participant. Until now, many meetings ran without a clear structure and often lasted longer than planned.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce fixed meeting rules so that our regular meetings run more productively in future. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> clear rules would do our meeting culture good, because currently many participants don't arrive on time, and the moderator has to make a real effort to keep the agenda on track.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> a fixed agenda and limited speaking time make it easier to stick to the agenda items. In addition, the moderator could record the outcome more clearly at the end and hold a vote if needed.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that not every discussion fits into a rigid time limit: whoever has to explain a complex topic sometimes simply needs more speaking time.

<r>That is why I propose that</r> the moderator should be able to grant extra speaking time — the more complex the topic, the more flexibility they should have. I would also find it useful to keep hybrid meetings with video conferencing, so that everyone stays up to date.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
David

topic.en: Mandatory conflict management training

task.en: Management is planning to introduce mandatory conflict management training for all employees, after tensions and unresolved conflicts arose in several departments. Until now, there have been no uniform rules for how to handle conflicts in the workplace.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you've probably already heard</r>, management is planning to introduce mandatory conflict management training for all employees. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this kind of training is really necessary, because lately some colleagues act as if there were no tension in the team at all, even though the tone is often already inappropriate.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> many misunderstandings simply escalate during a conflict because nobody wants to take responsibility. A mediator could step in early in such cases and find a fair solution.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that a single training session is hardly enough to permanently defuse escalating tensions if nothing changes about the overall workplace climate.

<r>That is why I propose that</r> regular feedback meetings also be introduced, so that everyone can give feedback early and voice criticism constructively before a misunderstanding turns into an open dispute.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Nina

topic.en: Standardized handover report when changing roles

task.en: Management wants to introduce a standardized handover report for all employees, to be filled out when changing positions or before a longer leave. Until now, there have been no fixed guidelines for how a task handover should be documented.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce a standardized handover report for all employees. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> everyone should clearly take responsibility for their own tasks, because until now the state of the work often remained unclear when someone changed positions or went on leave.
<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> the state of the work is much easier to follow with a fixed form, because the successor immediately gets an overview of open and completed tasks.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that an additional form sometimes feels tedious, and the actual purpose — namely staying calm instead of leaving tasks unresolved — can easily get lost in the process.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> each team clearly define who is responsible for which part of the handover, and that open points be raised regularly in a shared task list.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Alex

topic.en: Guidelines for positive email communication

task.en: Management has noticed that many internal emails are worded too negatively or unfriendly, which often leads to misunderstandings. That's why guidelines for positive and appreciative email communication are to be introduced.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce guidelines for positive and appreciative email communication, so that our workplace becomes more pleasant overall. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> these guidelines really make sense, because several colleagues recently told me that the tone in some internal emails is often too harsh and not very appreciative.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> many misunderstandings can be avoided by formulating the subject line and salutation more clearly from the start and consistently cc'ing important people.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that not everyone immediately shows understanding for new guidelines, especially when the suggested phrasing feels too formal or impersonal.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> we collect a few example phrases together, in order to avoid misunderstandings from the outset while still remaining factual and diplomatic.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Mark

topic.en: New company profile – more values, not just numbers

task.en: Management wants to completely revise the company profile on the corporate website, placing greater emphasis on the company culture and values. Until now, the focus has mainly been on market position with figures on revenue and profit.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to completely revise the company profile on our website and place greater emphasis on the company culture. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this revision is long overdue, because our company is often judged online only by revenue and profit, even though there is much more to us as an employer.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> our company culture can hardly be expressed in pure numbers, but rather becomes visible through concrete examples from everyday work and the employees' values.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that a convincing mission statement cannot be written overnight, but must be carefully prepared and coordinated with management.

<r>That is why I propose that</r> employees from different departments be actively involved in the process, so that the new company profile really authentically reflects our values and core competencies.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Julia

topic.en: New trade fair presence – more personal consulting

task.en: Management is planning to redesign the trade fair presence for the next industry fair, focusing more on personal consulting rather than pure promotional materials. Until now, the focus has mainly been on give-aways and brochures at the booth.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to redesign our trade fair presence for the next industry fair, focusing more on personal consulting rather than pure promotional materials. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> our booth should stand out more through personal consulting in the future, instead of scoring mainly with give-aways and brochures.
<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> every visitor could be advised individually if we spent less time simply handing out brochures.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that things often get hectic during the trade fair and there isn't always enough booth staff available to devote extensive time to every trade visitor.

<r>That is why I propose that</r> we develop a short, structured consulting conversation with three fixed questions, so that even during a full rush we can quickly spark visitors' interest and make contact.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Nina

topic.en: Standardized structure for product presentations

task.en: Management wants to introduce a standardized structure for internal presentations for the new product's market launch, with a fixed introduction, main part and conclusion, as well as mandatory diagrams to illustrate product features. Until now, each department has designed its presentations completely freely.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce a standardized structure for internal presentations for our new product's market launch. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> a standardized structure is, as we all know, a good idea in principle, because until now every department has organized its presentations completely differently, and the audience had to reorient itself every time.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> especially with complex product features, diagrams and statistics help to keep an overview and clearly illustrate the main advantages over our competitors.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that it is not always easy to structure every presentation exactly the same way when the products differ greatly in content.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> the new guidelines not be a rigid corset, but only offer a rough framework with an introduction, main part and conclusion that each department can fill flexibly.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
David

topic.en: Team spirit as a criterion in performance reviews

task.en: Management is considering officially adding team spirit as a criterion in the annual performance review, so that collaboration and team spirit are recognized more strongly. Until now, mainly individual performance has been evaluated.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is considering officially adding team spirit as a criterion in the annual performance review in future. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> this change is really overdue, because in everyday life some colleagues act as if teamwork were a pure waste of time, even though shared goals concern all of us.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> collaboration runs much more smoothly when roles and tasks within the team are clearly assigned and everyone knows exactly what they are responsible for.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that an official evaluation might create uncomfortable pressure: the more strongly team spirit is assessed, the more some colleagues might just want to appear helpful on the surface.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> we jointly develop clear, fair criteria by communicating openly with each other regularly and giving each other honest feedback as equals.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Anna

topic.en: Standardized guide for customer phone calls

task.en: Management is planning to introduce a standardized guide for customer phone calls, including a fixed greeting formula and clear rules on availability and callbacks. Until now, each department has handled calls differently.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce a standardized guide for customer phone calls. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> it is really about time we handled phone calls uniformly, because until now every department has handled calls quite differently, and some customers didn't even know in the end who they were actually speaking to.
<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> no customer should feel like they've been misconnected or have to wait a long time for an answer anymore.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that it is not always easy to forward a call correctly right away without leaving the customer waiting in the queue for a long time.

<r>That is why I propose that</r> we agree on a short, friendly greeting formula with name and department. Especially at the beginning of each phone call, it is decided whether the customer feels well looked after.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Alex

topic.en: Rules for respectful discussions in the team

task.en: Management wants to introduce fixed rules for discussions in the team, so that different opinions can be expressed respectfully and conflicts resolved constructively. Until now, there have been no clear guidelines for this, and some discussions have been rather chaotic.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce fixed rules for discussions in the team, so that different opinions can be expressed respectfully. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> such rules are really helpful, because when an opinion is well-founded, it should also be listened to calmly instead of being interrupted right away.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> not only the discussions themselves, but also the results would become much clearer, because everyone could present their position in a structured way.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that fixed rules might intimidate some colleagues: whoever doesn't dare to openly disagree in the first place might end up contributing even fewer of their own arguments.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> we make an effort to give everyone enough room to speak and to weigh the pros and cons together before a final decision is made.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Mark

topic.en: Mandatory checklist for online conferences

task.en: Management wants to introduce a mandatory checklist for online conferences, with which microphone, camera and internet connection should be tested before every meeting. Until now, technical problems have frequently occurred, costing valuable time.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce a mandatory checklist for online conferences. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.

<r>I am of the opinion that</r> such a checklist really makes sense, because the more often the connection is interrupted in the middle of a conversation, the more time we all lose and the more frustrated the whole team becomes.

<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> many technical problems can be avoided if we test the microphone, camera and internet connection a few minutes beforehand, in order to prevent such interruptions from the outset.

<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that not every problem can be solved by testing everything beforehand, because sometimes the connection simply drops in the middle of the conversation anyway.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> we all prepare a bit better for technical problems, for example by having a backup headset and the technical support contact details ready at hand.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Julia

topic.en: Standardized template for business correspondence

task.en: Management wants to introduce a standardized template with a fixed letterhead and clear rules for salutations and closing formulas for external business correspondence. Until now, each department has formatted emails according to its own taste, and some texts came across as stiff or bureaucratic.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,

<r>as you probably already know</r>, management is planning to introduce a standardized template with a fixed letterhead and clear rules for salutations and closing formulas for external business correspondence. <r>I would also like to write something on this topic in our blog today</r>.
<r>I am of the opinion that</r> such a template would really be helpful, because this is not just about formalities, but also about making a professional first impression on our customers.
<r>A very important argument in favor is that</r> standardizing the salutation and closing formula ensures more consistency, so that our emails appear uniform from an outside perspective.
<r>On the other hand</r>, one should also consider that fixed rules are indeed helpful, but should not end up making our emails sound like pure bureaucratic jargon.
<r>That is why I propose that</r> when creating the new template, we base ourselves on concrete examples regarding tone and word choice, so that the texts feel inviting instead of off-putting.
<r>What do you think about this? I'm curious to hear your opinion.</r>
Nina

topic.en: More decision-making leeway for discounts in offers

task.en: Management is considering whether sales staff should be allowed to decide on discounts and special conditions in offers themselves in future, within a set framework, without having to consult management every time. Until now, every discount had to be approved individually.

parts.en: Dear colleagues,
