explanation.en:
In German, the verb always has a fixed place in the sentence — its position immediately shows whether a clause is a main clause or a subordinate one.
In a main clause, the conjugated verb is always in position 2 — no matter what comes before it.
In a subordinate clause (after dass, weil, wenn, ob, etc.), the conjugated verb moves all the way to the end instead.
Example: Weil er krank ist, bleibt er zu Hause.
Because he is sick, he stays home.
— here „ist“ is not in position 2, but right at the end, because the sentence starts with „weil“.

rule.en:
1. Main clause: verb in position 2
In a German main clause, the conjugated verb always stands in position 2 — no matter what occupies position 1 (subject, time expression, object, etc.). This is called verb-second order.

Ich lese heute ein Buch.
I'm reading a book today.
(position 1: subject)
Heute lese ich ein Buch. (position 1: time expression — the subject shifts to position 3!)
Ein Buch lese ich heute. (position 1: object)

Important: only one sentence element ever stands before the verb — no matter how long it is.

2. Subordinate clause: verb at the end
After subordinating conjunctions such as dass, weil, wenn, ob, obwohl, während, nachdem, bevor, da, damit, sodass, als, the conjugated verb moves all the way to the end of the clause.

Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
I'm staying home because I'm sick.
Sie fragt, ob er morgen kommt.
She asks whether he's coming tomorrow.

3. Sentence bracket with two verb parts
When there are two verb parts (perfect tense, modal verb + infinitive, separable verb), they form a sentence bracket (Satzklammer): the conjugated part stands at the front, the second part at the very end.

Main clause: Ich habe das Buch gelesen.
I have read the book.
Main clause: Ich muss das Buch lesen.
I must read the book.
Main clause: Ich rufe dich morgen an.
I'll call you tomorrow.

Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich das Buch gelesen habe.
Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich das Buch lesen muss.
Subordinate clause: ..., weil ich dich morgen anrufe.

4. Questions
Yes / no question — verb in position 1: Kommst du morgen?
Are you coming tomorrow?
Wh-question — question word in position 1, verb in position 2: Wann kommst du?
When are you coming?

explanation.en:
To negate something in German, you use either „nicht“ or „kein“ — which one you choose depends on what exactly you're negating.
„Kein“ negates a noun that has an indefinite article or no article at all:
Ich habe keine Zeit.
I have no time.

„Nicht“ negates everything else — a verb, an adjective, or the whole sentence — and often stands at the end:
Er kommt heute nicht.
He isn't coming today.

rule.en:
1. Kein — negating the noun
Kein replaces the indefinite article „ein / eine“ or negates a noun that has no article at all (plurals, uncountable nouns). It's declined exactly like „ein“.

Ich habe einen Bruder. → Ich habe keinen Bruder.
I have no brother.

Ich trinke Kaffee. → Ich trinke keinen Kaffee.
I don't drink coffee.

Das sind Probleme. → Das sind keine Probleme.
These are not problems.

2. Nicht — negating everything else
Nicht negates verbs, adjectives, adverbs, nouns with a definite / possessive article, and whole sentences.

CaseRule
Sentence negation„nicht“ usually stands right at the end of the sentence
Er kommt heute nicht.
He isn't coming today.
Partial negation„nicht“ stands directly before the word being negated
Er kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.
He's not coming today, but tomorrow.

3. Nicht with verbs that have a preposition / prefix
With verbs that have a fixed preposition or a separable prefix, „nicht“ usually stands right before them:
Ich interessiere mich nicht für Politik.
I'm not interested in politics.

Er ruft mich nicht an.
He doesn't call me.

4. Fixed expressions
In fixed expressions with no article, „kein“ remains the standard even where you might expect „nicht“:
Ich habe keine Ahnung.
I have no idea.

Ich habe keine Lust.
I don't feel like it.

explanation.en:
Some German connectors come in two parts that work together to link two parts of a sentence — you can't use one half without the other.
The most important ones:
„entweder...oder“ either...or, one of two options,
„sowohl...als auch“ both...and, both together,
„weder...noch“ neither...nor, none of the two,
„nicht nur...sondern auch“ not only...but also, more than expected,
„zwar...aber“ indeed...but, a limitation.
Example:
Sowohl mein Kollege als auch ich waren dabei.
Both my colleague and I were there.

rule.en:
Overview of the most important two-part connectors

ConnectorMeaning
entweder ... oderone of two possibilities
Entweder wir fliegen, oder wir fahren mit dem Zug.
Either we fly, or we take the train.
sowohl ... als auchboth together, no contrast
Sie spricht sowohl Deutsch als auch Französisch.
She speaks both German and French.
weder ... nochneither of the two options (double negation)
Er hat weder Zeit noch Lust.
He has neither time nor the desire.
nicht nur ... sondern auchmore than expected, escalation
Er ist nicht nur pünktlich, sondern auch zuverlässig.
He's not only punctual, but also reliable.
zwar ... aberconcession + restriction
Zwar ist das Projekt teuer, aber es lohnt sich.
The project is indeed expensive, but it's worth it.

1. Word order with „entweder“, „weder“, „zwar“
If the first part stands right at the front of the sentence, it counts as position 1 — the verb follows directly after it (position 2):
Entweder kommt er heute, oder er kommt gar nicht.
Either he comes today, or he doesn't come at all.

2. „Weder ... noch“ negates doubly
No extra „nicht“ is needed — the negation is already contained in „weder / noch“:
Er kann weder kochen noch backen.
He can neither cook nor bake. (incorrect: „Er kann nicht weder kochen noch backen.“)

3. Comma rule
Before „oder“, „als auch“, and „noch“ there is usually no comma, since these link items in a list — before „aber“ and „sondern“, however, a comma is required because a contrast follows:
Zwar regnet es, aber wir gehen trotzdem raus.
It's raining, but we're going out anyway.

title.en: um zu / ohne zu / (an)statt zu + infinitive

explanation.en:
These three constructions link an infinitive clause to the main clause — but they only work when both clauses share the same subject.
„Um...zu“ states a goal or purpose (what for?):
Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen.
I study in order to pass the exam.

„Ohne...zu“ states something missing or not happening (without doing what?):
Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden.
He left without saying goodbye.

„(An)statt...zu“ states an alternative (instead of what?):
Sie arbeitet, anstatt zu schlafen.
She works instead of sleeping.
If the main and subordinate clause have different subjects, you need „damit“, „ohne dass“, or „anstatt dass“ instead.

rule.en:
1. Basic condition: the same subject
Infinitive constructions with „zu“ only work when the main clause and the subordinate part share the same subject. If not, you need the corresponding subordinate-clause variant with „dass“.

ConstructionQuestion / other variant
um ... zuWhat for? With what goal?
other variant: damit
ohne ... zuWithout doing what?
other variant: ohne dass
(an)statt ... zuInstead of doing what?
other variant: anstatt dass

2. Examples with the same subject (infinitive with zu)
Ich lerne, um die Prüfung zu bestehen. (I study = I pass the exam)
Er ging, ohne sich zu verabschieden. (he left = he doesn't say goodbye)
Sie arbeitet, anstatt zu schlafen. (she works = she doesn't sleep)

3. Examples with different subjects (dass-clause)
Ich gebe dir das Buch, damit du es liest. (I give / you read — two different subjects)
Er ging, ohne dass jemand es bemerkte.
He left without anyone noticing.

Sie arbeitet weiter, anstatt dass die anderen ihr helfen.
She keeps working instead of the others helping her.

4. Position of „zu“ with separable verbs
With separable verbs, „zu“ goes between the prefix and the stem:
um die Prüfung abzuschließen
in order to complete the exam

title.en: Comparative clauses: als, wie, je…desto / umso

explanation.en:
German has three different words for making comparisons — which one you use depends on whether the things are equal, unequal, or change together proportionally.

„Wie“ compares equal things:
Er ist so groß wie sein Vater.
He is as tall as his father.

„Als“ compares unequal things with a comparative:
Er ist größer als sein Vater.
He is taller than his father.

„Je...desto / umso“ + comparative shows that as one thing increases, the other increases (or decreases) too:
Je mehr er übt, desto besser wird er.
The more he practices, the better he gets.

Note: after „je“ the verb goes to the end, after „desto“ normal word order applies with the verb in position 2.

rule.en:
Overview
WordType / adjective form after it
wieequality (so ... wie)
after it: positive form
alsinequality
after it: comparative form
je ... desto / umsoproportionality
after it: two comparatives

1. Wie — equality
Pattern: so + adjective (positive form) + wie.
Er ist so groß wie sein Vater.
He is as tall as his father.

Negated:
Er ist nicht so groß wie sein Vater.
He isn't as tall as his father.

2. Als — inequality
After a comparative, it's always „als“, never „wie“:
Er ist größer als sein Vater.
He is taller than his father. (not: „größer wie“ — a common colloquial mistake!)

3. Je ... desto / umso — proportionality
Two clauses are linked: the first (with „je“) is a subordinate clause — verb at the end. The second (with „desto“ / „umso“) is a main clause with the verb in position 2, right after „desto / umso + comparative“.

Je mehr er übt, desto besser wird er.
The more he practices, the better he gets.

Je früher wir anfangen, umso schneller sind wir fertig.
The earlier we start, the sooner we'll be done.

Note: „desto“ and „umso“ are interchangeable — same meaning, „umso“ sounds slightly more formal.

4. Common mistake
„Wie“ after a comparative is colloquially incorrect:
Er ist größer wie ich
→ correct: Er ist größer als ich.
He is taller than me.

explanation.en:
The little word „es“ has several functions in German that at first glance seem to have nothing to do with each other.
First: as an impersonal pronoun for weather, time, or fixed expressions:
Es regnet.
It's raining.
Second: as a placeholder for a subject or a dass-clause that comes later in the sentence:
Es freut mich, dass du kommst.
It makes me happy that you're coming.
Third: as a correlate, which points ahead to a subordinate clause (verb at the end):
Ich finde es toll, dass du kommst.
I think it's great that you're coming.
Important to know: in these cases „es“ often carries no meaning of its own — it only fulfills a grammatical function.

rule.en:
1. Es as an impersonal pronoun
With weather, time of day, and some fixed expressions there's no „real“ subject — „es“ fills that slot:
Es regnet.
It's raining.
Es ist spät.
It's late.
Es gibt viele Möglichkeiten.
There are many options.
Es geht mir gut.
I'm doing well.
This „es“ never disappears, not even when word order changes: Heute regnet es.
Today it's raining.

2. Es as a placeholder (Vorfeld-es)
When the actual subject (often a dass-clause or infinitive) doesn't yet stand at the start of the sentence, „es“ stands as a placeholder in position 1 — it disappears as soon as something else takes position 1.

Es freut mich, dass du kommst. → Dass du kommst, freut mich. (no more „es“!)
It makes me happy that you're coming. → That you're coming makes me happy.
Es ist wichtig, pünktlich zu sein. → Pünktlich zu sein ist wichtig.
It is important to be punctual. → Being punctual is important.

3. Es as a correlate (always stays)
With certain verbs (es geht um, es kommt an auf, es handelt sich um) „es“ is a fixed part of the expression and always stays in the sentence, no matter what is in position 1:
Es geht um Geld.
It's about money.
In diesem Text geht es um Geld.
This text is about money.

4. Test: does „es“ disappear when reordering?
If „es“ disappears when something else takes position 1 → placeholder-es.
If „es“ stays → correlate or impersonal pronoun.

explanation.en:
„Wer“ doesn't just start a question (Wer kommt? Who's coming?); it can also start a subordinate clause (verb at the end) with no reference word — that is, no noun in front that „wer“ points back to (as in „der Kollege, der ...“). It then means „whoever...“ or „the one who...“.
Wer zu spät kommt, verpasst den Zug.
Whoever comes late misses the train.
The main clause after it often begins with „der“, „den“ or „dem“, which points back to „wer“ once more: Wer fragt, der lernt.
Whoever asks, learns.
Whether it is „der“, „den“ or „dem“ depends on the role the word plays in the main clause (nominative, accusative or dative).

rule.en:
1. Structure: wer-clause + correlate clause
A „wer“-clause is a subordinate clause (verb at the end) that needs no reference noun and means „the one who...“. It is followed by a main clause that often begins with an article word (der / den / dem) referring back to „wer“ — the correlate.

Wer zu spät kommt, verpasst den Zug.
Whoever comes late misses the train.
Wer fragt, der lernt.
Whoever asks, learns.

2. The correlate follows the case in the main clause
The correlate takes whatever case it needs in the main clause.

CaseCorrelate
Nominativeder
Wer fragt, der lernt.
Whoever asks, learns.
Accusativeden
Wer zu spät kommt, den lässt man nicht mehr rein.
Whoever comes late is no longer let in.
Dativedem
Wer clever ist, dem gelingt es leicht.
Whoever is clever finds it easy to succeed.

3. „wer“ has case forms of its own
„wer“ changes too: wer (nominative), wen (accusative), wem (dative) — depending on its role in the subordinate clause. So the case of „wer“ and the case of the correlate are independent of each other.

Wem das nicht passt, der kann gehen.
Whoever doesn't like it can leave.
(„wem“ = dative in the subordinate clause, „der“ = nominative in the main clause)

4. The correlate can also be dropped
If the correlate is nominative, it's often left out: Wer zu spät kommt, verpasst den Zug. (instead of: ..., der verpasst den Zug.)

5. Similar construction with „was“
„Was“ works the same way for things / generalizations: Was er sagt, das stimmt.
What he says is true.

explanation.en:
German has fixed combinations of a noun and a fairly „empty“ verb that together mean roughly the same as one simpler verb.
You can't guess the meaning from the individual parts — you have to learn the whole combination as a unit.

Examples:
„in Kraft treten“ to take effect,
„Anwendung finden“ to be applied,
„zur Verfügung stehen“ to be available.

These noun-verb collocations are typical of formal and professional texts — in everyday speech, people would often just say:
„gelten“ to apply,
„anwenden“ to apply / use,
„verfügbar sein“ to be available.

rule.en:
1. What is a noun-verb collocation (NVV)?
A fixed combination of a noun (usually with a preposition) + a semantically „empty“ verb (treten, finden, stehen, kommen, bringen, geben, nehmen ...). The meaning often corresponds to a single full verb.

NVVMeaning
in Kraft tretengelten
to take effect
Das Gesetz tritt am 1. Januar in Kraft.
The law takes effect on 1 January.
Anwendung findenangewendet werden
to be applied
Die neue Methode findet breite Anwendung.
The new method is widely applied.
zur Verfügung stehenverfügbar sein
to be available
Der Berater steht Ihnen zur Verfügung.
The consultant is at your disposal.
eine Entscheidung treffenentscheiden
to decide
Der Vorstand trifft die Entscheidung.
The board makes the decision.
in Betracht ziehenerwägen
to consider
Wir ziehen diese Option in Betracht.
We are considering this option.

2. Why does it matter?
NVVs are typical of formal, professional, and written texts (reports, contracts, news) and sound noticeably more stylistically confident at B2 / C1 level than the plain full verb.

3. Remember the fixed preposition and article
With NVVs, the preposition and article (or its absence) are fixed — nothing can be swapped: zur Verfügung stehen (not „an der Verfügung“), in Kraft treten (not „auf Kraft“).

4. Passive with NVV
NVVs can also be used in a passive-like way with „werden“:
Die Entscheidung wird getroffen.
The decision is made.

explanation.en:
When the action matters more than the person doing it, German uses the passive voice or a passive substitute.
The true passive is formed with „werden“ + past participle:
Das Auto wird repariert.
The car is being repaired.

But there are also three alternatives with a similar meaning:
„sich lassen“ + infinitive: Das lässt sich reparieren — it can be repaired,
„sein + zu“ + infinitive: Das ist zu reparieren — it must / can be repaired,
a man-construction: Man repariert das Auto — one / they repair the car.

Important: who performs the action is often not mentioned at all in any of these forms — and that's exactly the point of the passive voice.

rule.en:
1. The true dynamic passive
Formation: werden (conjugated) + past participle (at the end of the clause). It describes a process, not the result.

TenseExample
PresentDas Auto wird repariert.
The car is being repaired.
Simple pastDas Auto wurde repariert.
The car was repaired.
Present perfectDas Auto ist repariert worden.
The car has been repaired.
With modal verbDas Auto muss repariert werden.
The car must be repaired.

2. Naming the agent: von / durch
If you do want to name the person performing the action, use „von“ (person / originator) or „durch“ (means / cause):
Das Auto wird von einem Mechaniker repariert.
The car is repaired by a mechanic.
Der Schaden wurde durch den Sturm verursacht.
The damage was caused by the storm.

3. Passive substitutes — three alternatives with modal meaning
FormMeaning
sich lassen + infinitivepossibility (can be)
Das Problem lässt sich lösen.
The problem can be solved.
sein + zu + infinitivepossibility OR necessity
Das Problem ist zu lösen.
The problem is to be / can be solved.
man + active clauseneutral, everyday style
Man löst das Problem.
One solves the problem.

4. Why use the passive / passive substitute?
Typical of reports, instructions, and scientific texts, when the focus is on the action or the object rather than on the person carrying it out.

explanation.en:
Sometimes you want to talk about people or quantities without naming them exactly — that's what indefinite pronouns are for in German.

For people:
„man“ someone, in general,
„jemand“ some unspecified person,
„niemand“ no one.

For things / quantities:
„etwas“ something,
„nichts“ nothing,
„alle“ everyone / all,
„jeder“ everyone / each,
„einige“ some,
„manche“ some, certain ones.

Just like articles and nouns, these pronouns are also declined — depending on their role in the sentence (subject, object, etc.):
Ich habe niemanden gesehen.
I didn't see anyone. (accusative case)

rule.en:
1. For people
PronounMeaning
mansomeone, in general
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: man / einen / einem
jemandan unspecified person
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: jemand / jemanden / jemandem
niemandno person
Nom. / Acc. / Dat.: niemand / niemanden / niemandem

„Man“ is never declined like a normal pronoun — in the accusative / dative it becomes „einen“ / „einem“:
Das ärgert einen wirklich.
That really annoys you / one.
In everyday speech, „jemand“ / „niemand“ can also drop the -en / -em endings:
Ich habe niemand(en) gesehen.
I saw no one.

2. For things and quantities
PronounMeaning
etwas / nichtssomething / nothing (invariable)
Declension: no endings
alleall (plural)
Declension: like the definite article
jedereach one (singular)
Declension: like „dieser“
einige / manchean indefinite quantity
Declension: like the definite article (plural)

3. Examples by case
Ich habe niemanden gesehen.
I saw no one. (accusative)

Ich habe allen geholfen.
I helped everyone. (dative)

Das interessiert jeden.
That interests everyone. (accusative)

4. Etwas / nichts + adjective
After „etwas“ and „nichts“, an adjective is capitalized and declined as after „ein-“ words:
etwas Interessantes — something interesting,
nichts Neues — nothing new.

title.en: als ob / als wenn + Konjunktiv II

explanation.en:
When you make a comparison that doesn't match reality — that is, someone acts „as if“ something were true — German requires Konjunktiv II.
„Als ob“ or „als wenn“ introduce this unreal comparative clause, and the verb goes in Konjunktiv II:
Er tut, als ob er alles wüsste.
He acts as if he knew everything.
(In reality, he doesn't know everything.)
You can also drop „ob“ / „wenn“ — then the verb comes right after „als“:
Er tut, als wüsste er alles.

rule.en:
1. Two variants: with and without „ob“ / „wenn“
ConstructionWord order
als ob / als wennsubordinate clause: verb at the end
Er tut, als ob er alles wüsste.
He acts as if he knew everything.
als (alone)verb right after „als“
Er tut, als wüsste er alles.
He acts as if he knew everything.

Both variants mean the same thing — the short form with „als“ + verb (word order as in a main clause) is somewhat more elegant / literary.

2. Why Konjunktiv II?
The comparison doesn't match reality — you're expressing: „He acts this way, but in reality it's different.“ This is the typical use of Konjunktiv II for unreal situations.

3. Present vs. past
Time referenceForm
PresentKonjunktiv II Präsens
Sie tut, als ob sie krank wäre.
She acts as if she were sick.
PastKonjunktiv II Perfekt
Sie tut, als ob sie krank gewesen wäre.
She acts as if she had been sick.

Präsens: the simple form or „würde“ + infinitive.
Perfekt: „hätte“ / „wäre“ + past participle.

4. Common verbs in this construction
sein → wäre,
haben → hätte,
können → könnte,
wissen → wüsste,
kommen → käme.
For most other verbs, spoken German uses „würde“ + infinitive:
als ob er schlafen würde.
as if he were sleeping.

explanation.en:
Besides the regular passive (with „werden“), German has the stative passive with „sein“ — it doesn't describe the process, but the resulting state.
Compare:
Die Tür wird geöffnet. (process — someone is opening it right now)
Die Tür ist geöffnet. (state — it's already open, the result of the action)
It's formed with „sein“ + past participle, and you use it when you want to describe the current state after a completed action, not the action itself.

rule.en:
1. Two types of passive compared
TypeFormation
Dynamic passive (Vorgangspassiv)werden + past participle
Meaning: process, action underway
Die Tür wird geöffnet.
The door is being opened.
Statal passive (Zustandspassiv)sein + past participle
Meaning: state, result of the action
Die Tür ist geöffnet.
The door is open.

2. The test: „happening right now“ vs. „already done“
Can you insert „right now“? → dynamic passive. Are you only describing the state afterward, with no one actively performing the action? → statal passive.

Das Geschäft wird um 8 Uhr geöffnet. (Process: someone opens it at 8 o'clock.)
Das Geschäft ist ab 8 Uhr geöffnet. (State: it's open from 8 o'clock on, regardless of who opened it.)

3. Tenses of the statal passive
TenseExample
PresentDer Laden ist geschlossen.
The shop is closed.
Simple pastDer Laden war geschlossen.
The shop was closed.
Present perfectDer Laden ist geschlossen gewesen.
The shop has been closed.

4. No agent (no „von“ phrase)
In the statal passive, you almost never name who performed the action — the focus is exclusively on the subject's current state.

explanation.en:
A good text isn't just a series of unrelated sentences — the sentences need to be connected to each other so the text flows and makes sense.
There are several tools for this: connectors, pronouns, synonyms, and picking up terms mentioned earlier.
Especially important are small reference words that point back to something mentioned before:
„dabei“ in doing so / in this context,
„dadurch“ through this fact,
„dazu“ in relation to this,
„davon“ about this / of this,
„damit“ by this means.
They replace repeating the previous part of the sentence:
Die Firma wächst. Dabei hilft die neue Strategie.
The company is growing. The new strategy helps with that.

rule.en:
1. Devices for linking a text together
DeviceFunction
Connectorslogical link between sentences
deshalb, außerdem, jedoch
Pronounsreplace a noun already mentioned
er, sie, es, dieser
Synonymsavoid repeating a word
die Firma → das Unternehmen
da-compoundsrefer back to a whole situation
dabei, dadurch, dazu, davon, damit

2. The da(r)-compounds in detail
These words replace „preposition + that (thing mentioned)“ and refer to the whole preceding sentence or situation, not just to a single noun.

Die Firma wächst. Dabei hilft die neue Strategie.
The company is growing. The new strategy helps with that.
Er hat viel gearbeitet. Dadurch hat er Erfolg gehabt.
He worked a lot. Because of that, he was successful.
Wir planen ein Projekt. Ich freue mich darauf.
We're planning a project. I'm looking forward to it.

3. Rule: „dar-“ is used before a vowel
If the preposition begins with a vowel, „dar-“ is used instead of „da-“: darauf, darüber, darin (instead of „da-auf“).

4. Why does it matter for B2 / C1 texts?
These reference words make a text more compact and avoid constantly repeating whole parts of a sentence — typical of good reports and essays.

explanation.en:
When you want to explain HOW (by what means) something was achieved, German uses a modal clause with „dadurch, dass“ or „indem“.
Both essentially ask: „In what way?“ or „By what means?“
„Indem“ is the shorter, more common form:
Er lernte die Sprache, indem er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.
(The method was: reading a lot.)
„Dadurch, dass“ means the same thing, but puts a bit more emphasis on the fact as the means: Er lernte die Sprache dadurch, dass er viel las.

rule.en:
1. Two forms for „in what way?“
ConnectorStyle
indemshorter, more common
Er lernte die Sprache, indem er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.
dadurch, dassmore formal, stresses the means
Er lernte die Sprache dadurch, dass er viel las.
He learned the language by reading a lot.

Both are subordinate clauses — the conjugated verb stands at the end: ..., indem er viel las.

2. Distinguishing from „weil“
„Weil“ states a reason / cause (why?), while „indem“ / „dadurch, dass“ state a means / method (by what means, in what way?). Compare:
Er ist müde, weil er viel gearbeitet hat.
He's tired because he worked a lot. (reason)
Er wurde erfolgreich, indem er viel gearbeitet hat.
He became successful by working a lot. (method)

3. Common mistake: „durch“ + noun instead of „indem“ + clause
„Durch“ + noun is a preposition (not a subordinate clause):
Durch viel Lesen lernte er die Sprache.
By reading a lot, he learned the language.
But if you need a full clause with a verb, „indem“ is required: indem er viel las.

4. Position in the sentence
The „indem“-clause can stand before or after the main clause; if it comes first, the main clause verb follows directly after it (position 2):
Indem er viel las, lernte er die Sprache.
By reading a lot, he learned the language.

title.en: Fixed prepositions with nouns / verbs / adjectives

explanation.en:
Certain verbs, nouns, and adjectives in German „require“ one specific preposition — you can't choose freely; you have to memorize it together with the word.
This is called government (Rektion):
sich interessieren für + accusative (not „an“ or „über“),
stolz sein auf + accusative — proud of,
Angst vor + dative — afraid of.

Tip: always learn such combinations as a whole unit — not just „interessieren“, but „sich interessieren für“ right away — then the right preposition comes automatically.

rule.en:
1. Verbs with a fixed preposition (examples)
VerbPreposition + case
sich interessierenfür + acc.
Ich interessiere mich für Kunst.
I'm interested in art.
wartenauf + acc.
Ich warte auf den Bus.
I'm waiting for the bus.
sich freuenüber + acc. / auf + acc.
Ich freue mich über das Geschenk. / auf die Reise.
I'm happy about the gift. / I'm looking forward to the trip.
denkenan + acc.
Ich denke an dich.
I'm thinking of you.

2. Adjectives with a fixed preposition
AdjectivePreposition + case
stolzauf + acc.
Sie ist stolz auf ihre Arbeit.
She's proud of her work.
zufriedenmit + dat.
Er ist zufrieden mit dem Ergebnis.
He's satisfied with the result.

3. Nouns with a fixed preposition
NounPreposition + case
die Angstvor + dat.
Angst vor der Prüfung
fear of the exam
das Interessean + dat.
Interesse an Sprachen
interest in languages

4. Important
„An“, „auf“, „über“ don't change their case depending on meaning here — with governed prepositions (Rektion), the case is fixed, regardless of the usual two-way preposition rule (Where? = dative, Where to? = accusative).

5. Learning tip
Always learn these as a whole unit: not just „warten“, but „warten auf + acc.“ — ideally together with an example sentence.

explanation.en:
When reporting what someone else said, German can use Konjunktiv I to signal: „This isn't my own statement — I'm just reporting what was said.“

This is especially typical of news reports:
Er sagte, er sei krank.
He said he was sick. (instead of: er ist krank)

A practical problem: for many verbs, Konjunktiv I looks exactly like the indicative (e.g. with „ich“, „wir“, „sie / plural“) — in these cases, speakers switch to Konjunktiv II instead, so it stays clear that this is reported speech.

rule.en:
1. Formation of Konjunktiv I
Present-tense stem + endings: -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en. Only „sein“ is irregular: ich sei, du seist, er / sie / es sei, wir seien, ihr seiet, sie seien.

Verber / sie / es
sagener sage
habener habe
könnener könne

2. When does Konjunktiv I → Konjunktiv II?
With „ich“, „wir“, and „sie“ (plural), Konjunktiv I often looks exactly like the indicative (e.g., „ich sage“, „sie sagen“) — so in those cases speakers switch to Konjunktiv II to keep reported speech recognizable:
Sie sagten, sie würden kommen.
They said they would come. (instead of „sie kommen“, which wouldn't be recognizable as a subjunctive)

3. Time relationships
Time referenceForm
SimultaneousKonjunktiv I Präsens
Er sagt, er sei müde.
He says he is tired.
PriorKonjunktiv I Perfekt
Er sagt, er sei müde gewesen.
He says he was tired.

Perfekt: „habe“ / „sei“ + past participle.

4. Verbs that introduce reported speech
Typical after: sagen, behaupten, berichten, erklären, betonen, meinen — often with „dass“ or without it (in which case main-clause word order applies):
Er sagte, dass er krank sei. / Er sagte, er sei krank.
He said he was sick.

explanation.en:
In formal German — especially in reports, instructions, or official texts — verbs are often turned into nouns. This is called nominalization.

There are two ways to do it:
an ending like „-ung, -nis“: prüfen → die Prüfung
to check → the exam,

a nominalized infinitive with a capital letter and the article „das“: prüfen → das Prüfen
the checking.

Why does it matter? A nominal style sounds more factual and compact — typical of reports:
„Nach Abschluss der Prüfung...“
After the completion of the exam...
instead of
„Nachdem die Prüfung abgeschlossen wurde...“
After the exam was completed...

rule.en:
1. Two ways to nominalize a verb
MethodFormation
Derivation with a suffixverb stem + -ung / -nis, etc.
prüfen → die Prüfung, ankommen → die Ankunft
the check, the arrival
Nominalized infinitiveinfinitive, capitalized, with „das“
prüfen → das Prüfen, lesen → das Lesen
the checking, the reading

2. Typical conversion: subordinate clause → noun phrase
An entire subordinate clause with a conjunction (nachdem, weil, wenn) can often be shortened to a preposition + nominalization — typical of formal style.

ClauseNominal style
Nachdem die Prüfung abgeschlossen wurde, ...
After the exam was completed...		Nach Abschluss der Prüfung, ...
After completion of the exam...
Weil die Kosten gestiegen sind, ...
Because costs have risen...		Wegen des Anstiegs der Kosten, ...
Due to the rise in costs...
Wenn man die Regeln beachtet, ...
If one follows the rules...		Bei Beachtung der Regeln, ...
When observing the rules...

3. Genitive instead of the clause's subject / object
What was the subject or object in the subordinate clause becomes a genitive attribute in nominal style:
die Kosten steigen — costs rise
→ der Anstieg der Kosten — the rise in costs.

4. When to use it?
Typical of reports, scientific texts, instructions, and official / administrative language — in everyday spoken German, nominal style often sounds too stiff.

explanation.en:
Modal particles are small, unchangeable words used mainly in spoken German — they don't change the content of a sentence, only how it sounds or is meant.
They usually can't be translated directly; they express an attitude, a tone, or a mood.
„Doch“ contradiction / emphasis,
„ja“ a known fact,
„mal“ casual, relaxing,
„eben / halt“ that's just how it is,
„denn“ friendly interest in questions,
„schon“ reassurance / confidence.
Example:
Komm doch mal vorbei!
Do come by sometime!
This sounds much more inviting than the bare „Komm vorbei!“

rule.en:
Overview of the most important modal particles

ParticleEffect
dochcontradiction, emphasis, reminder
Das weißt du doch! / Komm doch mit!
You know that, don't you! / Do come along!
jaa known, obvious fact
Das ist ja toll!
That's really great!
malcasual, softens a request
Komm mal her. / Zeig mal!
Come here a sec. / Show me!
eben / halt„that's just how it is, nothing to be done“
Das ist eben so. / So ist es halt.
That's just how it is. / That's just the way it is.
dennfriendly interest (only in questions)
Wie geht es dir denn?
So how are you doing?
schonreassurance, confidence
Das wird schon klappen.
It'll work out, don't worry.

1. Position in the sentence
Modal particles stand in the middle field of the sentence — usually right after the conjugated verb (and pronouns), never at the start of the sentence.

2. Combinations are possible
Several particles can appear together and reinforce the tone:
Komm doch mal vorbei!
Do come by sometime!
(a friendly invitation, softer than plain „Komm vorbei!“)

3. Meaning differs by sentence type
„Doch“ in statements = emphasis / reminder; „doch“ as an answer to a negative question = contradiction:
Kommst du nicht mit? — Doch!
Aren't you coming along? — Yes, I am!

4. Why does it matter at B2 / C1?
Without modal particles, spoken German often sounds unnaturally stiff — using them correctly makes the language authentic and idiomatic.

explanation.en:
Participles are verb forms that can be placed in front of a noun and declined just like regular adjectives.
Participle I (active, formed with „-end“): describes something happening right now — „das lachende Kind“ = a child who is (currently) laughing.
Participle II (mostly passive or completed): describes the result of an action — „das gebackene Brot“ = bread that has (already) been baked.
Just like any adjective before a noun, the participle also gets the matching adjective ending.

rule.en:
1. Partizip I — active, simultaneous
Formation: infinitive + „-d“ (lachen → lachend). Describes what is happening right now, usually from the perspective of the person performing the action:
das lachende Kind
the child who is currently laughing
der schlafende Mann
the sleeping man

2. Partizip II — mostly passive, completed
Formed the same way as in the perfect tense (ge-...-t / ge-...-en). Describes the result of an action (usually one the object underwent from outside):
das gebackene Brot
the bread that was baked
der reparierte Wagen
the repaired car

ParticipleMeaning
Partizip Iactive, happening right now
das lachende Kind
the laughing child
Partizip IIpassive / completed, result
das gebackene Brot
the baked bread

3. Declined like a normal adjective
Before a noun, the participle takes the usual adjective ending, depending on the article, case, and gender: der lachende Mann, die lachende Frau, dem lachenden Kind.

4. Extended participial construction
A participle can be expanded with further information and then stands entirely before the noun — typical of formal / written texts:
der vor Kurzem eingestellte Mitarbeiter
the employee hired recently
(instead of: der Mitarbeiter, der vor Kurzem eingestellt wurde)

explanation.en:
„Während“ is a word with two quite different functions — you have to look at the sentence structure to tell which one is meant.
As a temporal connector, it introduces a subordinate clause:
Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik.
While he works, he listens to music.
(with its own verb in the subordinate clause)
As a preposition with the genitive, it stands directly before a noun:
während des Meetings
during the meeting
(no separate verb, just a noun in the genitive)
Other common genitive prepositions that work the same way:
„wegen“ because of — wegen des Regens,
„trotz“ despite — trotz der Kälte,
„aufgrund“ due to — aufgrund der Lage,
„innerhalb / außerhalb“ within / outside — innerhalb einer Woche.

rule.en:
1. „Während“ as a connector (subordinate clause)
Introduces a whole subordinate clause with its own verb — verb at the end of the clause:
Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik.
While he works, he listens to music.

2. „Während“ as a preposition + genitive
Stands directly before a noun in the genitive, with no verb of its own:
während des Meetings
during the meeting
während der Woche
during the week

FunctionFeature
Connectorown subordinate clause, verb at the end
Während er arbeitet, hört er Musik.
While he works, he listens to music.
Preposition + genitiveno verb, just a noun in the genitive
während des Meetings
during the meeting

3. Other genitive prepositions with the same structure
PrepositionMeaning
wegenreason
wegen des Regens
because of the rain
trotzconcession / contrast
trotz der Kälte
despite the cold
aufgrundreason (more formal)
aufgrund der Lage
on the basis of the situation
innerhalb / außerhalbtime / space-limited
innerhalb einer Woche
within a week

4. Colloquial usage: genitive prepositions + dative
In spoken German you'll often hear „wegen dem Regen“ (dative) instead of „wegen des Regens“ (genitive) — but in formal / written German and on exams, the genitive is always the standard.

topic.en: Description of an employer

task.en:
Describe an employer you have worked for or would like to work for
(e.g., industry, products and services, departments and their tasks, special features).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Company? Where?
Which industry?
Which department(s)?
What were my tasks?
What products or services were offered?
What was the working atmosphere like?
What was the boss like?
What were the colleagues like?
Challenges?
What did I like most about the company?
Further training? Professional development?

questions.en: Can you give me a specific example from your everyday work at this employer?

A good example is building the marketing and sales structure from scratch: we created marketing materials, developed a new website, and introduced clear sales processes. Already in the second month, this generated more revenue than the entire previous year.
Why did you choose this particular employer?
I was personally invited by the CEO and co-owner of the company to lead this young but loss-making department. The trust shown and the challenge convinced me right away.
What challenges did you face in this job, and how did you deal with them?
The biggest challenge was that there was practically neither marketing nor a structured sales system. So we had to build everything from scratch in a short time.
What did you like most about this employer?
What I liked most was working with creative people in an international environment, as well as the fast, measurable success of our work.
Was there also something you didn't like so much about this company?
In the early phase, there were hardly any fixed structures, so we had to improvise a lot. It was exhausting, but it also taught me a great deal.
What was the collaboration with your colleagues like?
The collaboration was very close and creative. Together with the team, we created the marketing materials, developed the website, and built up the sales processes.
What did you learn during this time that is still useful to you today?
During this time, I gained a great deal of practical experience — especially in how to build structures from scratch in a short time. This knowledge is still useful to me today.
Would you work for this employer again? Why or why not?
Yes, I would work there again. It was a very intense time that strongly shaped my professional development.
How does this employer differ from others you have worked for?
AIR is an international media company and an official YouTube partner in content and creator management. Compared to other employers, the environment was noticeably more international and creative.
What would you advise someone who wants to start working for this employer (or a similar company)?
I would advise being open to rapid change and ready to build structures from scratch. Anyone who wants to work in a creative, international environment will find many exciting opportunities there.

topic.en: A good working environment

task.en:
Describe how you imagine a good working environment
(e.g., job security, wages/salary, career opportunities, communication within the company, examples from your professional experience).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Job security?
Wages / salary?
What are the career opportunities like?
What is communication like in the company?
Working atmosphere?
Working hours?
Further training? Professional development?
What don't I want?
Where could this environment exist?
Examples from your professional experience

questions.en: Can you give me a specific example of a good working environment?

A good example is a team where all members share the same vision, are intrinsically motivated, are paid fairly, and show mutual appreciation. In such an environment, employees develop a real 'ownership mindset' and achieve outstanding results.
Why is this particular aspect of the working environment so important to you?
Because without shared values, no team can function sustainably in the long run. For me, shared values are the most important foundation on which everything else is built.
What experiences have you had yourself with a good or bad working environment?
I have seen myself that teams without a shared vision often stall, while teams where all three factors — motivation, pay, and appreciation — come together develop a real ownership mindset.
What would you do if the working environment didn't match your expectations?
I would address this openly and try to find solutions together with the leadership. If nothing changes in the long run, I would look for an environment that better matches my values.
How does a good working environment affect employee performance?
A good working environment greatly boosts employee motivation. When employees identify with the company and feel appreciated, a real ownership mindset develops, leading to outstanding results.
What is more important to you: a high salary or a good working atmosphere? Why?
For me, a good working atmosphere is the foundation, but without fair pay, financial security is missing, which is needed to fully focus on work. For me, both factors are inseparably linked.
In your opinion, what should communication between the boss and employees look like?
Communication between the boss and employees should be open, respectful, and characterized by mutual appreciation. Only in this way can trust and a real ownership mindset develop.
What would you do as a manager to create a good working environment?
As a manager, I would first make sure the team shares common values. Then I would focus on fair pay, intrinsic motivation, and regular appreciation, so that a real ownership mindset can develop.
Are there differences in the working environment between Germany and your home country?
I think the basic principles — shared values, motivation, fair pay, and appreciation — apply the same everywhere. Differences tend to lie more in how communication and hierarchy are practiced.
What would you advise someone who has a bad working environment?

I would advise first identifying which of the three factors is missing — motivation, pay, or appreciation — and having a conversation with leadership. If nothing changes, one should have the courage to make a change.

topic.en: Events and experiences that influenced the choice of profession

task.en:
Describe the events and experiences that influenced your choice of profession
(e.g., stages, important people, motivation, consequences).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Stages (school graduation, training / studies, …)
Dreams, aptitudes, talents
Important people for your career choice?
Motivation?
Consequences?
Would you choose this profession again?

questions.en: Can you name a specific event that influenced your choice of career?
A decisive event was attending a mathematics and physics lyceum, which greatly intensified my passion for exact sciences.
Which person had the greatest influence on your choice of career, and why?
The greatest influence came from my teachers at the mathematics and physics lyceum, who nurtured my fascination with mathematics, physics, and computers.
Were there also doubts or detours on your path to this profession?
Yes, after 17 years as an entrepreneur in Ukraine, I had to start completely from scratch in Germany and find my way in the IT field anew.
How has your motivation changed over time?
At first, my motivation was purely scientific; later, entrepreneurial ambition was added, and today I am mainly driven by the desire to develop as an SAP consultant.
What would you do differently in hindsight?
In hindsight, I might have started learning German earlier to make it easier to enter the German job market.
What consequences did this decision have for your future life?
The decision to study computer systems later enabled me to found my own company and gain extensive experience in management and business development.
What would you advise young people who are facing a similar career choice?
I would advise young people to follow their passion and dive early into fields like mathematics or IT, as this foundation opens many doors later.
How did your environment (family, friends) react to your decision?
My family supported my passion for exact sciences from the very beginning and encouraged me to attend the mathematics and physics lyceum.
What was the most difficult moment on this path?
The hardest moment was arriving in Germany, when I had to re-analyze the job market and translate my 17 years of experience into a new context.
Would you choose the same profession again today? Why?
Yes, I would choose this path again, because the combination of a technical foundation and entrepreneurial thinking is exactly what distinguishes me today as an aspiring SAP consultant.

topic.en: A professional role model

task.en:
Describe a person in your life who is a professional role model for you
(e.g., your relationship with this person, qualities, their influence on you).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Which person?
What is your relationship with this person?
What positive qualities does this person have?
What influence does / did this person have on you?

questions.en: Can you give me a specific example of how this person influenced you?
A concrete example is how my grandfather patiently explained everything to me as a child while we built and repaired things together, showing me that real knowledge comes from hands-on practice.
How often do you have contact with this person?
As a child, I had very close contact with him thanks to our summers together; even today, despite the distance, we stay connected through regular conversations.
Which quality of this person do you admire most, and why?
What I admire most is his curiosity — even at the age of 82, he learned how to use a smartphone.
Was there a situation where you particularly remembered this person?
I particularly remember the moment when, at 82, he proudly used his first smartphone — it showed me that you should never stop learning.
How exactly did this person influence your professional decisions?
His life motto that everything begins with a goal and the path to it can always be found still accompanies me in every professional decision.
What would you do to become more like this person?
I try to be as curious and persistent as he is, staying open to new things and not giving up too quickly.
Does this person also have weaknesses that you have noticed?
Like every person, he also had his weaknesses, but his strengths — curiosity, persistence, and the ability to inspire others — shaped me far more.
How does your role model differ from other people around you?
Unlike many other people in my life, he never stopped learning new things, even at an advanced age.
What would you say to this person if you had the chance?
I would tell him that his values — curiosity, persistence, and the ability to inspire others — still shape my professional decisions today.
Which piece of advice from this person have you taken to heart the most?
The phrase that influenced me the most is: everything begins with a goal — you will always find the way to it.

topic.en: Approach to job searching

task.en:
Describe the process of job searching for a country of your choice
(e.g., finding job offers, first contact, application documents or interview).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Where do you look for job offers? (newspaper, internet, job board, fairs)
What documents do you need?
What should be included in the cover letter?
What should be included in the CV?
How do you prepare for the job interview?

questions.en: Can you describe the job search process in this country in more detail?
In Germany, the job search usually begins with researching job portals like Indeed or the Federal Employment Agency, followed by a written application with a CV and cover letter.
What challenges are there when searching for a job in this country?
A major challenge is often the language requirements as well as the recognition of foreign degrees and qualifications.
How does job searching there differ from job searching in your home country?
In Germany, complete and formally correct application documents are much more important than in my home country, where personal contacts are often enough.
What role do personal contacts or networks play in the job search?
Personal contacts and networks, the so-called 'Vitamin B', also play an important role in Germany, especially at smaller companies.
What should you pay special attention to with application documents in this country?
You should pay attention to a complete application file with a CV, cover letter, and relevant certificates, as well as a professional application photo.
How long does it usually take to find a job?
Depending on the industry and qualifications, the job search in Germany can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months.
Which online platforms or resources would you recommend for job searching?
I would recommend platforms like the Federal Employment Agency, Indeed, StepStone, and LinkedIn.
What would you advise someone who is just starting their job search?
I would advise starting to prepare the documents early and researching the relevant industry specifically.
What mistakes should you avoid when searching for a job?
You should avoid incomplete or incorrect application documents, as well as insufficient preparation for interviews.
How important are language skills when searching for a job in this country?
Language skills are very important in Germany, as many employers expect at least a B2 level of German.

topic.en: What matters in a job interview

task.en:
Describe what matters in a job interview. Talk about a country of your choice
(e.g., professional field, preparation, clothing, typical questions).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Getting to the company?
For which profession?
How do you prepare?
Clothing?
Behavior?
Salary expectations?

questions.en: Can you give an example of a typical question in a job interview in this country?
A typical question in Germany is, for example: 'Why did you apply to us specifically?' or 'What can you contribute to our team's success?'
What is the best way to prepare for a job interview?
You should thoroughly research the company and understand how you can create real added value for the team using your own strengths.
What clothing is appropriate for a job interview in this country?
In Germany, clothing should match the desired role — usually neat and rather conservative, since, as they say, clothes make the man.
What are the biggest mistakes you can make in a job interview?
One of the biggest mistakes is insufficient preparation, which means you cannot convincingly explain why your profile represents added value for the team.
How important is the first impression in a job interview?
The first impression is decisive, as the first minutes of the conversation often shape the entire rest of it.
What questions should you ask the employer yourself?
You should ask questions that show you have researched the company, for example about its values or the challenges the team faces.
How do you deal with difficult or uncomfortable questions?
With difficult questions, it helps to stay calm and answer honestly rather than avoiding them.
What distinguishes a successful interview from an unsuccessful one?
A successful interview happens when both sides recognize the mutual value — then a job offer is just a matter of time.
How important is body language in a job interview?
Body language is very important, since a confident posture and a friendly presence make a significant difference.
What would you advise someone who is very nervous before a job interview?
I would advise preparing well and realizing that a job interview is not an exam, but a negotiation about a win-win situation.

topic.en: A minimalist learning app

task.en:
Describe a product / service of your choice
(e.g., features, benefits for customers, advantages and disadvantages, success).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Which product?
What features?
Where is it available?
Since when has the product existed?
What is it good for, or what benefit does it offer the customer?
Advantages?
Disadvantages?
Success?
Marketing? Changes?

questions.en: Can you describe the main features of this product/service in more detail?

The app is a minimalist learning app precisely tailored to the curriculum for levels A2, B1, and B2, combining scientific learning methods with gamification. It covers listening, reading, writing, and grammar.
What specific benefit does this product/service offer customers?
The greatest benefit for customers lies in targeted exam preparation, ease of use, and significant time savings.
What sets this product apart from similar offerings on the market?
Unlike most language apps that only offer general content, this app is specifically focused on a single goal and exam, so no time is wasted on unnecessary options.
What advantages and disadvantages does this product have, in your view?
A big advantage is that you can clearly focus on one learning goal; a possible disadvantage is that the app currently only covers levels A2 to B2.
How successful is this product/service on the market?
Since the product is currently free and ad-free, I can't yet give concrete revenue figures, but user feedback has been very positive so far.
Which target group is this product particularly suited for?
This app is particularly suited for people who want to prepare specifically and quickly for a German exam.
How has this product developed over time?
So far, I have mainly developed the app's content further, to align it even more precisely with the curriculum for the levels.
What would you improve about this product if you could?
I would like to add further language levels as well as additional interactive exercises.
How is this product advertised or marketed?
Currently, the product is mainly promoted through the address mova.now and personal recommendations.
Would you recommend this product to others? Why or why not?
Yes, I would recommend the app, as it helps users save valuable time and prepare specifically for their exam.

topic.en: Business idea: a learning app

task.en:
You want to become self-employed. Describe your business idea
(e.g., what product/service, special features, target group).

tips.en:
Possible questions:
Become self-employed doing what?
Own company?
Which industry?
How to attract customers?
How did you come up with this idea?
Do you need employees?
How to finance it?
Where is support available?
Are there already similar ideas / companies?

questions.en: Can you describe your business idea in a bit more detail?
My business idea is a mobile learning app called mova.now for immigrants, precisely tailored to exam preparation for levels A2, B1, and B2.
Who is the target group for your product or service?
The target group is mainly immigrants who want to prepare specifically and efficiently for a German exam.
What makes your business idea special or unique?
What's special is that the app combines scientific learning methods with gamification and is available in four languages, which sets it apart from classic textbooks and general language apps.
What challenges do you expect when implementing this idea?
A major challenge will be turning a free offering into a viable business model while competing with established language learning apps.
How do you plan to finance your business?
Initially, I want to finance the project with my own savings, and later possibly look for grants or investors for further development.
What competition already exists in the market?
There are already several language learning apps on the market, but most of them offer only general content instead of targeted exam preparation.
How do you plan to attract customers' attention to your offer?
I want to attract customers' attention mainly through personal recommendations, social media, and cooperation with language schools.
What role does sustainability or digitalization play in your business idea?
Digitalization plays a central role, since the entire learning platform works on mobile devices without any physical materials.
What would be your first step in implementing this idea?
My first step would be to continue testing the product and gather feedback from the first users in order to improve it in a targeted way.
How do you imagine your business in five years?
In five years, I imagine having turned this project into a successful business in Germany and having become fully self-employed here.
